title: What is Pause and Play?
body: Pause and Play is a companion app for perimenopause and beyond. It brings together practical tools for foggy moments, calming practices for overwhelming ones, and playful challenges for when you need a lift. It was developed with a clinical advisory panel of registered health professionals, so every tool is grounded in evidence. It isn't a medical service and doesn't diagnose or treat anything. Think of it as a kind, clever friend in your pocket who helps you get through the day, understand what's happening, and feel a bit more like yourself.

title: Who is Pause and Play for?
body: Pause and Play is made for women in perimenopause, menopause and the years after, whether symptoms are mild or turning life upside down. It's also helpful if menopause has come early, after surgery or cancer treatment. You don't need a diagnosis or to be on any treatment to use it. Partners, friends and family are welcome to explore the Learn section too, because understanding what's going on makes it much easier to support someone you love.

title: The three parts of Pause and Play
body: The home screen is built around three ideas. Practical tools help when your brain is juggling too much, like saving your place or remembering where you put things. Calming moments help when you feel overwhelmed or can't switch off. Playful challenges give you a quick laugh or a small win. Underneath, Support and tracking lets you map moods, manage medicine reminders, track your cycle and learn more. Start with whatever you need right now. There's no wrong door.

title: Is Pause and Play a medical app?
body: No. Pause and Play offers education, skills and encouragement. It doesn't diagnose, assess or treat any condition, and it won't tell you which medicine to take or how much. Your GP, pharmacist or specialist is the right person for those decisions. What the app can do is help you notice patterns, keep track of reminders, feel calmer and prepare for appointments, so the time you spend with your doctor is more useful.

title: How Pause and Play keeps humour kind
body: You'll find gentle humour throughout the app, like hunting for glasses that are on your head. The rule we follow is simple: we laugh at the situation, never at you. Perimenopause can be frustrating and exhausting, and a knowing smile can take some of the sting out of it. If something ever feels dismissive rather than relieving, we'd genuinely like to know, because what feels light to one person can land differently for another.

title: Your privacy in Pause and Play
body: Your information belongs to you. Pause and Play stores data securely in Australia, never sells it and never uses it for advertising. Tracking tools like Mood Mapper, Medicine Cabinet and Cycle Tracker ask for your consent before you start. You can download everything you've logged, or delete your account and all your data, from Settings at any time. Voice notes are turned into text and the audio isn't kept. Only the text you choose to save is stored.

title: Free and Plus
body: All six everyday tools, Sprout, the trackers and a selection of Learn content are free. Pause and Play Plus is an optional membership that adds extras like a guided audio library, monthly expert masterclasses and the full Learn library. Content marked PLUS will show a small badge. You can see your current plan in Settings. Nothing essential for your safety or wellbeing, like crisis information, is ever behind a paywall.

title: The Pause and Play program
body: The Pause and Play program is an 8-week guided program. Each week includes a short video, a simple workbook and a daily practice, with live group sessions led by qualified facilitators and guest sessions from health professionals. Topics include sleep, the anxious moments, mood and the low days, brain fog, identity and who you're becoming, relationships, and building your own plan. It's education and skills in a supportive group, not individual therapy. You can join the waitlist from the clinical panel page.

title: What Pause and Play is not
body: Pause and Play isn't therapy, a crisis service or a replacement for your GP. It can't respond in an emergency, and Sprout is an AI guide rather than a person. If you're struggling a lot, or things feel unsafe, please reach out to real people. Call Lifeline on 13 11 14 any time, or 000 in an emergency. Your GP can also talk with you about support, including seeing a psychologist.

title: Accessibility in Pause and Play
body: Pause and Play is designed to be easy on tired eyes and busy brains. Text uses a typeface chosen for readability, buttons are large, and nothing important depends on colour alone. You can speak instead of typing using Tell Sprout. Animations calm down automatically if your device is set to reduce motion, and the app works in light or dark mode. If anything is hard to use, let us know so we can improve it.

title: Using Pause and Play on your phone
body: Pause and Play works in your phone's browser, and you can add it to your home screen so it opens like any other app. On an iPhone, open it in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. On Android, open the browser menu and choose Install app or Add to Home screen. Once installed, reminders can reach you as notifications, if you choose to turn them on in Settings.

title: Feedback and ideas
body: Pause and Play is shaped by the women who use it. If a tool helps, if something feels off, or if there's a topic you wish we covered, we'd love to hear it. Questions Sprout can't answer are noted anonymously so our clinical team can consider adding new information to the library. That's how the app grows to reflect what women are actually asking about.

title: What do you need right now?
body: The home screen starts with one simple question: what do you need right now? Instead of making you hunt through menus, it offers tools based on how you feel. Foggy? Try a practical tool. Overwhelmed? Choose a calming moment. Flat or frazzled? Pick a playful challenge. Perimenopause can make decisions feel harder than usual, so the app does the sorting for you. Just tap the one that fits.

title: Side Quest Saver: what it is
body: Side Quest Saver is for those moments when you're interrupted mid-task and lose the thread. You write down what you were doing and the very next step, and add a gentle nudge if you like. Your original mission waits safely while you handle the side quest. When you come back, you can pick up exactly where you left off instead of starting from scratch.

title: Side Quest Saver: why it helps in perimenopause
body: Many women notice their working memory feels less reliable during perimenopause. Holding a half-finished task in your head while juggling interruptions is tiring. Writing it down moves that load out of your mind and onto the page, which psychologists call externalising. Naming the very next step matters most, because a small, specific action is much easier to restart than a vague job. It's a simple habit that saves real frustration.

title: Side Quest Saver tips
body: Keep the next step tiny and concrete, like find the rego number rather than sort out the car. Use a nudge when you know you'll get distracted, such as in 30 minutes. Tick missions off when they're done; that little moment of completion is worth noticing. And if you have several parked, start with the one that's quickest. Momentum builds confidence, and confidence makes the next one easier.

title: The Very Important Thing Department
body: The Very Important Thing Department is your searchable record of where important things live: the passport, the spare key, the good scissors, the car in the shopping centre car park. File a thing and its location, then search it later in seconds. It's open 24 hours and asks no questions. You can add items by typing or by voice through Tell Sprout.

title: Why the VIT Department helps
body: Misplacing things is one of the most common and most annoying parts of midlife brain fog. Your memory isn't failing; it's busy, and stress, poor sleep and hormonal changes all make everyday recall harder. Giving important items a fixed home and writing that home down means less searching and much less self-blame. Over time, the act of filing things also strengthens the habit of putting them back.

title: My brain has 37 tabs open
body: This tool is for when everything feels urgent at once. It starts with a one-minute breathing pause, with an optional grounding exercise. Then you close illustrated tabs, like dinner again or that email from work, until only one remains. That last tab is your one next action. Everything else can wait. It turns a swirl of worries into a single, doable step.

title: Why 37 tabs works
body: When we feel overloaded, stress narrows our focus and makes choosing harder, so we freeze or rush between tasks. A slow breath out helps settle the body's stress response. Then choosing one action gives your mind somewhere to land. Psychologists use similar ideas in problem-solving and stress management. It's not about getting everything done. It's about getting unstuck enough to do the next thing.

title: Help me wind down
body: Wind-down is the quiet corner of Pause and Play. The screen dims, the petal counter hides, and there are no scores, streaks or rewards. Choose a short session, like one for the 3am mind, a cooling body scan for night sweats, or a gentle muscle relaxation. You can turn the screen off and simply listen. A guided audio library, developed with our clinical advisory panel, will live here.

title: Why wind-down has no rewards
body: Most of Pause and Play gently celebrates your efforts, but the wind-down area deliberately doesn't. Points, sounds and pop-ups wake the brain up, which is the opposite of what you need at night. Sleep also can't be forced; trying hard to sleep often makes it harder. So these practices are about helping your body settle, so rest has a better chance of arriving. Nothing to win here. Just rest.

title: Give me a little win
body: Little win offers short, untimed puzzles like sorting the washing into lights and darks, or matching lost things to where they turned up. There's no timer and no penalty for getting something wrong, and every finish earns the same reward. It's designed for flat or foggy days when bigger tasks feel out of reach, giving you a quick sense of completion.

title: Why small wins matter
body: Finishing something small, even a game, builds a real sense of capability. On low or flat days, motivation often comes after action rather than before it, so a small, achievable task can help shift your mood a little. This idea is part of a well-researched approach called behavioural activation. A little win won't fix a hard day, but it can be a gentle first step.

title: I need a laugh
body: I need a laugh offers everyday scenes to sort out, like finding the glasses that have been on her head all along, or auditing a handbag with seven receipts and three lip balms. The jokes laugh at the situation, never at you. It's a quick, light break for when you need reminding that you're far from the only one living this.

title: Why laughter helps
body: Laughing at a situation, rather than at yourself, takes some of the sting out of it. Humour can ease tension, lift mood for a moment and help you feel connected to others going through the same thing. It also offers some perspective when frustration is running high. Of course, laughter isn't a treatment. It's simply a kind pause that can make a hard moment feel a little lighter.

title: Tell Sprout: speak instead of type
body: Tell Sprout lets you say what you need to remember instead of typing it. Tap the mic and say something like I'm booking the dentist, next I need my Medicare card, or my passport is in the top drawer. Sprout sorts it into Side Quest Saver or the Very Important Thing Department, and shows you what it heard so you can check it before saving.

title: Why voice entry helps
body: When your hands are full or your brain is crowded, typing can be the barrier that stops you writing something down. Speaking is faster and takes less effort, so you're more likely to capture the thought before it slips away. Sprout always shows you the text before saving, because voice recognition can mishear. Your voice is turned into text and the audio isn't kept.

title: Who is Sprout?
body: Sprout is a friendly AI guide in Pause and Play, drawn as a little seedling in a pot. Sprout can point you to the right tool and share information from the Pause and Play library, which is reviewed by our clinical advisory panel. Sprout is not a person and not a therapist. It can't give medical or personal advice, and if you're in distress it will share crisis contacts straight away.

title: What Sprout can and can't do
body: Sprout can explain common perimenopause and menopause experiences, describe treatment options in general terms, help you find a tool, and suggest questions for your GP. Sprout can't tell you what to take, change a dose, interpret test results, diagnose symptoms or respond in an emergency. When something needs a health professional, Sprout will say so. If Sprout doesn't know, it will tell you honestly rather than guess.

title: Mood Mapper: how it works
body: Mood Mapper lets you log how you feel in two taps. Choose one of four squares: wired and tense, bright and buzzing, low and flat, or calm and content. Then, only if you want to, add feeling words, what's going on inside and around you, and a short note or voice note. Over time, a colour strip shows your last two weeks at a glance.

title: Mood Mapper: why it helps
body: Moods in perimenopause can feel unpredictable, which can be unsettling. Tracking helps you step back and notice patterns, such as poor sleep days often being tense days, or walks often going with calmer moods. Noticing isn't diagnosing; it's information you can use, like protecting sleep before a big week. Psychologists often use mood diaries for exactly this reason. Patterns can also be helpful to share with your GP.

title: Mood Mapper: the four squares
body: The four squares map two things: how much energy you have and how pleasant you feel. Wired and tense is high energy but unpleasant, like irritable or anxious. Bright and buzzing is high energy and pleasant. Low and flat is low energy and unpleasant, like sad or tired. Calm and content is low energy and pleasant. Picking a square is quicker than finding the perfect word.

title: Mood Mapper: things you might notice
body: After a few days of logging, Mood Mapper may show simple observations, like on five of six days you tagged poor sleep, you also logged a tense or low mood. These are for reflection, not diagnosis, and they don't mean one thing caused another. You know your life best. Use them as clues, and if low days are sticking around, your GP is a good person to talk to.

title: Medicine Cabinet: what it does
body: Medicine Cabinet keeps your medicines and supplements in one place and reminds you when they're due. You enter each one exactly as your prescriber or label says, choose how often you take it, and set reminder times. It handles tricky schedules, like a patch twice a week or capsules on some days of a cycle. It's reminders only; it never suggests medicines or doses.

title: Medicine Cabinet: schedule patterns
body: Menopausal hormone therapy can follow quite different schedules. Medicine Cabinet offers seven patterns: every day; certain days of the week, such as a patch changed Monday and Thursday; every few days; days on and days off in a cycle, such as 12 days in every 28; a start-up then ongoing schedule, such as daily for two weeks then twice weekly; a long-term device replacement date; and only when needed.

title: Medicine Cabinet: supply and repeats
body: You can track how much of a medicine you have left and get a nudge seven days before you run out. You can also count down the repeats left on a script, with a reminder to book a GP appointment when they're used up. Running out of a hormone treatment suddenly can bring symptoms back, so a little planning helps keep things steady.

title: Medicine Cabinet: if you miss a dose
body: Pause and Play won't tell you how to catch up on a missed dose, because the right answer depends on the medicine. Check the consumer medicine information leaflet that came with it, or ask your pharmacist, who can advise quickly and for free. If you miss doses often, it may be worth talking with your GP about a form or schedule that fits your life better.

title: Discreet mode
body: Discreet mode keeps your health private on your lock screen and in your calendar. Instead of showing medicine names, reminders say something like time for your evening routine. It's useful if others see your phone or share your calendar. You can turn it on or off in Settings at any time. It applies to Google Calendar events and the subscription link too, so shared calendars only show neutral labels.

title: Cycle Tracker: what it does
body: Cycle Tracker records your periods, spotting, flow and symptoms on a simple calendar. It shows days since your last period, your recent cycle lengths and how much they vary. In perimenopause cycles often become less predictable, so instead of a confident date, it shows a range. It doesn't predict fertility or ovulation, and it isn't a form of contraception. Fertility prediction is left out deliberately, because those features need medical regulation.

title: Cycle Tracker: why it's useful in perimenopause
body: Changes to your periods are often the earliest and most reliable sign of perimenopause. Periods may become shorter, longer, lighter, heavier or skip months. A record of these changes, along with symptoms, helps you and your GP see what's really happening rather than relying on memory. It can also help you spot things worth checking, like very heavy bleeding. Over a few months, the record often shows a pattern you'd never spot day to day.

title: GP summary
body: Before an appointment, you can create a one-page summary of your cycles, symptoms, medicines and mood patterns. You choose what to include. Bringing a clear record helps your doctor understand your experience quickly, especially when symptoms come and go. Health organisations recommend tracking symptoms for a few months and bringing that record to your GP. The summary is created when you ask for it and isn't stored on our servers afterwards.

title: Learn: videos, articles and quizzes
body: Learn is the library of Pause and Play. It has short videos and articles developed with our clinical advisory panel, medically reviewed information on physical health topics, and quick quizzes to test what you know. Filter by type or topic, like sleep, mood, brain fog, body or treatment questions. Some items are part of Plus and show a small badge. Finishing a quiz earns petals for taking part, whatever your score.

title: Today
body: Today pulls the important bits of your day into one simple list: medicines due, your next parked side quest, reminders and, if you connect it, events from your calendar. Tick medicines off as you go. Keeping everything in one place means fewer apps to check and less to hold in your head. If nothing is due, Today simply says so, and you can enjoy the space. You can connect a calendar any time from Settings.

title: Connecting your calendar
body: You can connect Google Calendar so your events show up in Today, and choose whether Pause and Play adds your reminders to a separate Pause and Play calendar. It never changes your existing events. Apple Calendar and Outlook users can subscribe to a private link instead. Connect or disconnect any time in Settings, and discreet mode keeps medicine names out of your calendar.

title: Choosing your notifications
body: You decide what Pause and Play tells you about. In Settings, switch on or off medicine reminders, side quest nudges, a daily mood check-in, cycle reminders, daily motivation, new articles, weekly clinical insights from our panel and program news. You can set quiet hours, bundle non-urgent messages into a morning digest, and limit how many you get. Fewer, kinder notifications tend to be more helpful.

title: Your garden and petals
body: Every time you use a tool to look after yourself, you earn petals, and your garden grows from seedling to sprout, bud, bloom and eventually a wildflower meadow. Rewards are the same whether a puzzle goes smoothly or not, and there are no petals for taking medicines or for having good moods. The garden is simply a gentle way to notice your own efforts.

title: Badges
body: Badges celebrate trying something new, like parking your first side quest, closing tabs down to one, or finding the glasses. They're never about performance or perfection. You can see your badges on the home screen. Collect them if you enjoy it, or ignore them completely. Either way is fine. There are no leaderboards and no comparisons with anyone else. Badges are simply small, private nods to the steps you've taken for yourself.

title: Meet the panel page
body: The Meet the panel page introduces the clinical advisory panel behind Pause and Play: the registered health professionals who review our tools, articles and the Sprout library. You'll also find the principles behind how the app is built, information about the 8-week program, who owns and runs Pause and Play, and a reminder about where to find more support if an app isn't enough. Reach it any time from the home screen.

title: Why this helps notes
body: Each tool has a fold-out note called Why this helps, written by the Pause and Play clinical team and reviewed by our advisory panel. It explains the psychology behind the tool in a couple of sentences. Understanding why something works often makes it easier to use and to stick with, and it's a reminder that these aren't just games but skills grounded in evidence. Tap the note under any tool's heading to open it.

title: Using the app on hard days
body: On hard days, keep it simple. Open the app and pick just one thing: park a task, breathe for a minute, or do a tiny puzzle. You don't need to log everything or use every feature. Small acts count. And if a hard day turns into many hard days, please consider talking with your GP or someone you trust. The wind-down area is a good place to land when you need quiet rather than another task.

title: Who reviews Pause and Play?
body: Pause and Play is developed with a clinical advisory panel of independent, registered health professionals. The panel includes a clinical psychologist, who reviews psychological and wellbeing content; a general practitioner with menopause training, who reviews medical content such as hormones, medicines and bleeding; and a pelvic health physiotherapist, who reviews bladder, pelvic floor and movement content. Nothing goes into the app, Learn or the Sprout library until the right panel member has approved it. You can meet the panel from the home screen.

title: Panel credentials
body: Every panel member is registered with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) in their profession. Their names, professions and registration details are listed on the Meet the panel page, so you can check them on the public register. Panel members only review content within their own expertise: psychological content goes to the psychologist, medical content to the GP, and pelvic health content to the physiotherapist. [Panel names and registration numbers to be added once agreements are signed.]

title: What is a clinical psychologist?
body: A clinical psychologist is a registered psychologist with advanced postgraduate training in assessing and treating mental health difficulties, such as anxiety, depression and stress. They use evidence-based therapies like cognitive behavioural therapy. Psychologists don't prescribe medication; that's the role of GPs and psychiatrists. In Pause and Play, the panel psychologist reviews how each tool supports your thinking, feelings and behaviour, while medical questions are always pointed back to your doctor.

title: Why Pause and Play exists
body: Many women arrive at midlife juggling work, family and ageing parents just as their bodies and minds start to change. Pause and Play was created to offer something practical and kind for the everyday moments in between appointments: the foggy mornings, the 3am wake-ups and the days when everything feels like too much. The aim is simple: clear information, useful tools and a little lightness, all checked by people who know what they're talking about.

title: How Pause and Play is built
body: Three principles guide everything. Grounded in evidence: tools draw on well-established approaches like cognitive behavioural therapy, behavioural activation and relaxation skills, adapted for real life at midlife. Skills, not diagnosis: Pause and Play teaches practical skills and never assesses, diagnoses or scores your symptoms. Humour with kindness: we laugh at the situation, never at you. Women deserve clear information, practical support and the reassurance that they're not the problem; this stage of life is just a lot.

title: How content is reviewed
body: Every article, tool explanation and Sprout library entry goes through the same steps. It's drafted by the Pause and Play content team, then reviewed by the panel member with the right expertise, and only published once they approve it. Physical health topics are always reviewed by a medical practitioner. Each item records who reviewed it and when, and content is checked again at least once a year, or sooner when guidelines change.

title: Can I see a panel member?
body: Pause and Play is an education and skills app, not a way to receive individual care from panel members. If you'd like one-to-one support, your GP is the best place to start. They can talk with you about a mental health treatment plan and a referral to a psychologist, which may attract a Medicare rebate, or a referral to another health professional. The Australian Psychological Society's Find a Psychologist service can also help you find someone near you.

title: Who owns Pause and Play?
body: Pause and Play is owned and operated by [Company] Pty Ltd, founded by Al [Surname]. The business is not owned by any of the health professionals on the clinical advisory panel. Panel members are independent advisers who are paid a fee to review content; they don't run the business day to day or make commercial decisions. Any family or financial relationship between a panel member and the owner is disclosed on the Meet the panel page.

title: What is perimenopause?
body: Perimenopause is the time leading up to your final period, when hormone levels, especially oestrogen and progesterone, rise and fall unpredictably. It starts when periods or symptoms begin to change and ends 12 months after your last period. In Australia it usually begins in your 40s, often around 47, and lasts about four to six years on average, though it can range from two to ten. Every woman's experience is different.

title: What is menopause?
body: Menopause is a single point in time: your final menstrual period. It's confirmed looking back, once you've gone 12 months without a period and there's no other cause. In Australia the average age is 51, and most women reach it between 45 and 55. Menopause happens because the ovaries stop releasing eggs and make much less oestrogen. People often use the word loosely for the whole transition.

title: What is postmenopause?
body: Postmenopause is the time after menopause, starting 12 months after your final period and continuing for the rest of your life. Some symptoms, like hot flushes, often ease over time, while others, such as vaginal dryness, can continue or appear later. Postmenopause is also a time to pay extra attention to bone and heart health, since lower oestrogen affects both. Many women describe this stage as freeing.

title: Premenopause versus perimenopause
body: Premenopause and perimenopause aren't the same thing. Premenopause is the time from your first period until perimenopause begins, when hormone cycles are generally regular. Perimenopause is a distinct phase with its own hormonal changes, which can cause physical, mental and emotional symptoms even while periods continue. Knowing the difference helps you recognise what's happening, rather than assuming it's too early to be hormonal.

title: Why hormones fluctuate in perimenopause
body: In perimenopause, the ovaries don't simply wind down smoothly. Oestrogen can swing higher and lower than usual from month to month, and progesterone tends to drop as ovulation becomes less regular. These ups and downs, rather than just low levels, explain why symptoms can come and go, and why one month can feel quite different from the next. It's not in your head. Your hormones really are changing.

title: How common are symptoms?
body: Experiences vary widely. Australian health information suggests about one in four women have few or no symptoms, about half have mild to moderate symptoms, and about one in four have severe symptoms that affect daily life. So if you're struggling, you're far from alone, and if you're sailing through, that's normal too. Whatever your experience, effective support and treatments are available.

title: Common signs of perimenopause
body: The most reliable early sign is a change in your periods: they may become shorter, longer, lighter, heavier or skip months. Other common signs include hot flushes and night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes, anxiety, brain fog, aches and pains, lower libido, vaginal dryness and bladder changes. Premenstrual symptoms can also get worse. Not every change is due to perimenopause, so it's worth checking with your GP.

title: Am I in perimenopause?
body: If you're in your 40s and notice changes to your periods, sleep, mood or temperature, perimenopause is a likely explanation. Doctors usually diagnose it based on your age, symptoms and period history, rather than a blood test. Tracking your cycles and symptoms for a few months gives a clearer picture. If you're under 45 and your periods change or stop, see your GP, as other causes need checking.

title: Do I need a blood test?
body: Usually not. For women over 45, doctors diagnose perimenopause and menopause from age, symptoms and period changes. Hormone levels swing so much during perimenopause that a single blood test can be misleading. Blood tests are useful if you're under 45, to check for early menopause or premature ovarian insufficiency, or to rule out other causes like thyroid problems or low iron. Home hormone and saliva tests aren't recommended.

title: Can I still get pregnant in perimenopause?
body: Yes. Even with irregular periods, you may still ovulate, so pregnancy is possible. Australian guidance generally recommends contraception until you've had two years without a period if you're under 50, or one year without a period if you're over 50. Hormone therapy for menopause is not a contraceptive. Your GP can help you choose a method that also suits your symptoms.

title: How long does it all last?
body: Perimenopause lasts about four to six years on average, but anywhere from two to ten is common. Hot flushes and night sweats often continue for several years; one large study found they lasted a median of about seven years overall, and longer for some women. Other symptoms, like vaginal dryness, may persist. The good news is that effective treatments exist, so you don't have to just wait it out.

title: Surgical menopause
body: Surgical menopause happens when both ovaries are removed, which causes an immediate drop in hormones rather than the gradual change of natural menopause. Symptoms can come on suddenly and be more intense. Removing the uterus alone (a hysterectomy without removing the ovaries) doesn't cause menopause straight away, though it can bring it on a little earlier. Your doctor can discuss treatment options, which often include hormone therapy.

title: Menopause after a hysterectomy
body: If you've had a hysterectomy but kept your ovaries, you won't have periods, so it's harder to tell when menopause happens. Symptoms like hot flushes, sleep changes or mood shifts are often the clues. Blood tests may be more useful in this situation. If you need hormone therapy and no longer have a uterus, oestrogen alone is usually used, as the progestogen part isn't needed.

title: Menopause is a natural transition
body: Menopause is a natural part of life, not an illness, and every woman who lives long enough will go through it. Natural doesn't mean you have to put up with symptoms that affect your work, relationships or wellbeing, though. Treatments and support exist precisely because this transition can be hard. Seeking help is a sensible, positive step, not a sign of weakness.

title: The menopause transition and life stage
body: Perimenopause often lands at an already busy time: careers peaking, children becoming teenagers or leaving home, parents ageing, relationships shifting. Hormonal changes can make these pressures feel heavier, and these pressures can make symptoms feel worse. Recognising that both are at play helps you be kinder to yourself and choose support for both your body and your life circumstances. Support for both can make a bigger difference than tackling either alone.

title: Every woman's menopause is different
body: Some women barely notice the transition; others find it life-changing. Age, genetics, overall health, stress, culture and life circumstances all shape the experience. Comparing yourself with a friend, sister or mother can be unhelpful, because your journey is your own. What matters is noticing what's happening for you, and finding the mix of information, support and treatment that fits. Your own record of symptoms is often more useful than anyone else's story.

title: Menopause in different cultures
body: Experiences and attitudes towards menopause vary across cultures. In some communities it's openly discussed and respected as a time of wisdom; in others it's rarely mentioned. The words used, the symptoms people notice and the support available can all differ. Jean Hailes and other Australian health organisations offer menopause information in many languages, and you can ask for an interpreter when seeing a health professional.

title: Menopause for trans and gender diverse people
body: Anyone with ovaries can experience perimenopause and menopause, including trans men and non-binary people, and the experience may interact with gender-affirming care. Trans women may have questions about hormone therapy as they age, too. Jean Hailes publishes perimenopause information written for trans and gender diverse people. A knowledgeable GP or specialist can help tailor information and treatment to your situation.

title: What happens to oestrogen after menopause?
body: After menopause, the ovaries make very little oestrogen. The body still makes a small amount in other tissues, such as fat. Lower oestrogen affects many parts of the body, including temperature control, sleep, the vagina and bladder, skin, bones and blood vessels. That's why menopause matters for long-term health, and why bone and heart checks become especially important in midlife.

title: Progesterone in perimenopause
body: Progesterone is made after ovulation each cycle. As ovulation becomes less regular in perimenopause, progesterone often falls earlier than oestrogen. This can contribute to heavier or irregular periods and, for some women, changes in sleep or mood. In hormone therapy, a progestogen is added for women who still have a uterus, to protect the lining of the womb from the effects of oestrogen.

title: Midlife is a great time for a health check
body: Australian health organisations suggest midlife, roughly 45 to 55, is an ideal time for a full health check, even if you feel well. It's a chance to review blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, weight, bone health risk, breast and cervical screening, and mental health. Since July 2025 there's a dedicated Medicare-rebated menopause and perimenopause health assessment with your GP. Ask for it by name when you book.

title: Hot flushes and night sweats
body: Hot flushes are sudden waves of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating and a racing heart. Night sweats are hot flushes during sleep. They're the most common menopausal symptoms, affecting around three in four women. They happen because falling oestrogen affects the brain's temperature control centre. Many effective treatments exist, both hormonal and non-hormonal.

title: Irregular periods
body: Changes to your periods are often the first sign of perimenopause. They might come closer together or further apart, be lighter or heavier, or skip months. This is usually normal in the transition. However, very heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods, bleeding after sex, or any bleeding after your periods have stopped should be checked by your GP. Tracking your cycle helps you spot changes.

title: Heavy periods
body: Some women have heavier periods during perimenopause, partly because hormone swings affect the womb lining. Heavy bleeding can lead to low iron, causing tiredness, breathlessness or feeling faint. Signs bleeding is heavy include soaking through pads or tampons every hour or two, passing large clots, or flooding. See your GP, as there are effective treatments and other causes may need checking.

title: Sleep problems
body: Sleep often changes in perimenopause. Night sweats can wake you, but many women also have trouble falling asleep or wake at 3am with a busy mind, even without sweats. Hormonal shifts, anxiety, needing to pass urine and life stress all play a part. Poor sleep then makes mood, concentration and coping harder. Good sleep habits, CBT for insomnia and hormone therapy can all help.

title: Mood changes
body: Mood changes like irritability, tearfulness, low mood, anxiety and feeling overwhelmed are common in perimenopause. Fluctuating oestrogen affects brain chemicals involved in mood, and poor sleep and life stress add to the load. Mood changes aren't universal, and they're not a personal failing. If low mood or anxiety lasts more than a couple of weeks or affects daily life, talk with your GP.

title: Anxiety
body: Some women experience anxiety for the first time in perimenopause, or find existing anxiety gets worse. It can show up as worry, restlessness, a racing heart, tension or a sense of dread. Hormonal changes, sleep loss and life pressures can all contribute. Breathing and grounding skills, CBT, exercise and medical treatments can help. If anxiety is affecting your life, your GP is a good first step.

title: Brain fog
body: Brain fog describes forgetfulness, trouble finding words, losing your train of thought and difficulty concentrating. Around six in ten women notice cognitive changes in the menopause transition. Research suggests these changes in memory and processing speed are usually temporary and tend to improve after menopause. Brain fog isn't a sign of dementia. Practical strategies, good sleep and managing stress can make a real difference.

title: Joint and muscle aches
body: Aches and pains in joints and muscles are common around menopause, and oestrogen changes may play a role. Staying active with low-impact exercise like walking, swimming or cycling, regular stretching, keeping a healthy weight and drinking enough water can help. Warm or cold packs and over-the-counter pain relief may ease discomfort. See your GP about new or worsening joint pain, as other conditions can cause it too.

title: Vaginal dryness and discomfort
body: Lower oestrogen can make vaginal and vulval tissues thinner, drier and less elastic, causing dryness, itching, burning or pain during sex. Doctors call this genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Unlike hot flushes, it often doesn't improve on its own and may gradually worsen. It's very treatable with moisturisers, lubricants and low-dose vaginal oestrogen, so it's worth raising with your GP even if it feels awkward.

title: Bladder changes
body: Menopause can affect the bladder and urethra, leading to needing to go more often, urgency, leaking or more frequent urinary tract infections. Urinary incontinence is common in midlife, but it's not something you have to live with. Pelvic floor training with a physiotherapist and vaginal oestrogen can both help. The National Continence Helpline, 1800 33 00 66, offers free advice from specialist nurses.

title: Lower libido
body: Changes in sexual desire are common at menopause. Vaginal dryness and pain, tiredness, stress, mood, relationship factors, body image and some medicines can all affect libido. Hormones are rarely the only factor. Talking openly with a partner, treating vaginal symptoms and looking after mental health can help. Your GP can discuss options, which may include hormone therapy or a referral to a psychologist with expertise in sexual concerns.

title: Palpitations
body: Some women notice a racing, pounding or fluttering heartbeat around menopause, sometimes with hot flushes or anxiety. Palpitations are often harmless, but they should be checked by a doctor, especially if they're new, frequent or come with chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or fainting. If you have chest pain or feel very unwell, call 000. Caffeine, alcohol, anxiety and low iron can also contribute, and your doctor can check for these.

title: Headaches and migraine
body: Hormone changes can affect headaches. Some women find migraines get worse during perimenopause when hormones fluctuate, then improve after menopause. Keeping a diary of headaches alongside your cycle and symptoms can reveal patterns. If you have migraines, mention them when discussing hormone therapy, as the type of treatment can matter. See your GP about any new, severe or unusual headaches.

title: Skin and hair changes
body: Lower oestrogen can leave skin drier, thinner and less elastic, and some women notice more wrinkles, itchiness or adult acne. Hair may thin on the scalp, and occasionally coarser hairs appear on the face. Gentle skincare, moisturiser, sun protection and not smoking help skin. If hair loss is significant, see your GP, as thyroid problems, low iron and other causes are worth checking.

title: Weight and body shape changes
body: Many women notice weight gain or a change in shape at midlife, with more fat around the tummy. Ageing, reduced muscle, lifestyle and life stress are major factors; menopause itself shifts where fat is stored rather than causing large weight gain. Strength training, regular activity, enough protein and good sleep all help. Hormone therapy doesn't cause weight gain. Focusing on strength, energy and wellbeing tends to be more helpful than chasing a number on the scale.

title: Fatigue and low energy
body: Feeling exhausted is common in perimenopause, often due to poor sleep, night sweats, heavy periods, stress or mood changes. Persistent tiredness is worth checking with your GP, as low iron, thyroid problems, depression and other conditions can cause it too. Small steps like regular movement, consistent sleep times and pacing yourself can help energy levels over time. Be patient with yourself; energy often improves as sleep and other symptoms are addressed.

title: Worse premenstrual symptoms
body: Some women find premenstrual symptoms like irritability, low mood, breast tenderness and bloating get worse in perimenopause, as hormone swings become larger. Some develop a more severe pattern called premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Tracking symptoms against your cycle can show whether they cluster before periods. If they're affecting your life, talk with your GP, as there are effective treatments. Planning lighter days when symptoms usually peak can also help.

title: Breast tenderness
body: Breast tenderness can happen in perimenopause when oestrogen levels swing high, and it can also be a temporary side effect when starting hormone therapy. It often settles over time. Any new breast lump, skin change, nipple change or discharge should always be checked promptly by your GP. Keep up with BreastScreen mammograms, which are free for women aged 50 to 74.

title: Dry eyes and dry mouth
body: Some women notice drier eyes or mouth around menopause, which may be linked to hormonal changes affecting moisture-producing glands. Eye drops, staying hydrated and taking screen breaks can help with dry eyes. See your GP or optometrist if symptoms persist, and your dentist about a dry mouth, as other causes and some medicines can be responsible too. Mention these symptoms when listing what's changed, as they're easy to overlook.

title: Feeling not like yourself
body: Many women describe perimenopause as a time when they don't feel like themselves: less confident, less patient, foggier or flatter. This can be unsettling and even a little frightening. It helps to know this is a common experience with real biological and life causes, and that it usually improves with time, support or treatment. You haven't lost yourself; you're in a big transition.

title: Symptoms that aren't menopause
body: Not every symptom in midlife is caused by menopause. Thyroid problems, low iron, diabetes, depression, sleep apnoea and side effects from medicines can all cause similar symptoms like tiredness, mood changes or sweating. That's why it's worth seeing your GP rather than assuming. A midlife health check can rule out other causes and make sure you get the right support.

title: Symptoms after menopause
body: For some women, hot flushes and night sweats continue well after menopause, sometimes for many years. Vaginal and bladder symptoms often become more noticeable over time, because they're linked to ongoing low oestrogen. You don't need to accept these as just part of getting older. Treatments remain available after menopause, so it's worth talking with your GP about what fits you.

title: Why hot flushes happen
body: Your brain has a temperature control centre in the hypothalamus. As oestrogen falls, this centre becomes more sensitive, so small changes in body temperature trigger a full cooling response: blood vessels widen, you flush and sweat, and your heart may race. Newer non-hormonal medicines work by calming the signalling in this exact area. Understanding the cause can make flushes feel less mysterious and less alarming.

title: How long hot flushes last
body: Hot flushes vary a lot. A large US study found the total duration was about seven years for many women, and some had them for longer, especially when they started early in perimenopause. Each flush usually lasts a few minutes. Frequency can range from a few a week to many a day. Effective treatment is available at any stage, so you don't need to wait for them to pass.

title: Treatments for hot flushes
body: Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. For women who can't or prefer not to use hormones, there are non-hormonal prescription options, including certain antidepressants, gabapentin and newer medicines that target the brain's temperature centre. Cognitive behavioural therapy and clinical hypnosis also have good evidence. Your GP can help you weigh up the options for you.

title: Cooling tips for the day
body: Dress in layers so you can peel one off quickly, and choose breathable natural fibres like cotton or linen. Carry a small fan or cooling spray, keep a cold drink nearby and sit near a window or air conditioning where you can. These won't stop flushes, but they can make them more comfortable and help you feel more in control when one arrives.

title: Cooling tips for the night
body: Keep your bedroom cool and well ventilated, and use lighter bedding in layers you can push off. Cotton or moisture-wicking sleepwear helps, and some women keep a spare set by the bed. A fan, a cool pack under the pillow or a glass of cold water within reach can help you settle again after a night sweat. Then try a slow breath out to ease back toward sleep.

title: Hot flush triggers
body: Some women find certain things bring on flushes or make them stronger, including alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot drinks, warm rooms, smoking and stress. Triggers differ between people, and research suggests avoiding them helps some women more than others. Logging flushes with Mood Mapper tags or notes for a couple of weeks can help you find your own patterns. Even small changes, like switching to iced drinks, can make a noticeable difference for some women.

title: What to do during a hot flush
body: When a flush starts, try to slow your breathing with a long, gentle breath out. Remind yourself it will pass in a few minutes. Loosen a layer, cool your wrists or neck and sip something cold. Many women find that feeling less embarrassed or anxious about flushes makes them easier to ride out. This is one of the ideas behind CBT for hot flushes.

title: CBT for hot flushes
body: Cognitive behavioural therapy has good evidence for reducing how much hot flushes and night sweats bother you and interfere with life. It combines understanding what's happening, managing stress, paced breathing during flushes, changing unhelpful thoughts like everyone is staring at me, and improving sleep habits. It's offered by psychologists and some programs. International menopause experts recommend CBT as a non-hormonal option.

title: Clinical hypnosis for hot flushes
body: Clinical hypnosis is a recognised non-hormonal option for hot flushes. In one well-known trial, women who had five weekly hypnosis sessions saw their hot flush frequency fall by about three quarters, compared with under a fifth in a control group, and many reported better sleep. Hypnosis here means guided relaxation and mental imagery, often of coolness, practised with a trained clinician.

title: Hot flushes at work
body: Hot flushes at work can feel especially exposing. It can help to sit near a window or fan, keep layers handy, have a cold drink at your desk and give yourself permission to step out briefly. Some women find a quick, matter-of-fact mention to colleagues takes the pressure off. You might also ask your manager about practical adjustments like temperature control or uniform options.

title: Night sweats and your partner
body: Night sweats can disrupt your partner's sleep as well as your own, which can add tension. Separate bedding, a fan on your side of the bed or even separate rooms for a while are practical solutions many couples use. Talking about it openly, with a bit of humour, helps both of you feel less frustrated and more like a team.

title: Waking at 3am
body: Waking in the early hours is very common in perimenopause. Night sweats, needing the toilet, hormone shifts and a busy mind can all play a part. Try not to clock-watch or tell yourself the next day is ruined. Breathe out slowly, let your body feel heavy, and if you're still wide awake after a while, get up and do something calm in dim light before trying again.

title: Good sleep habits
body: Keep regular sleep and wake times, even on weekends. Build a wind-down routine for the hour before bed: dim lights, screens down, something relaxing. Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet. Limit caffeine after midday and go easy on alcohol, which disrupts sleep later in the night. Get daylight and movement during the day. These habits help, though they may not be enough on their own.

title: CBT for insomnia
body: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, often called CBT-I, is the recommended first treatment for ongoing insomnia, and research supports it for women in menopause too. It usually includes setting a consistent sleep window, only going to bed when sleepy, getting up if you can't sleep, calming a racing mind and changing unhelpful beliefs about sleep. Psychologists, some GPs and digital programs offer it.

title: When your mind won't switch off
body: A busy mind at bedtime is common, especially when you're carrying a lot. Try a worry download before bed: write down what's on your mind and one next step for each, so your brain knows it's parked. Side Quest Saver works well for this. Then shift attention to your body, with slow breathing or a gentle body scan, rather than trying to force the thoughts away.

title: Trying too hard to sleep
body: Sleep is one of the few things that gets harder the more effort you put in. Lying in bed trying to sleep can create frustration that keeps you awake. Instead, aim to rest and let sleep arrive in its own time. If you've been awake and frustrated for a while, get up, do something quiet in low light, and return when you feel sleepy.

title: Naps
body: A short nap of 20 to 30 minutes early in the afternoon can help on a rough day without upsetting night-time sleep. Longer or later naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night, especially if you're having insomnia. If you find you need to nap every day, or feel very sleepy during the day despite enough time in bed, talk with your GP.

title: Sleep apnoea in midlife
body: The risk of obstructive sleep apnoea rises for women after menopause. Signs include loud snoring, gasping or choking at night, waking unrefreshed, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness. It's often missed in women because symptoms can look like menopause or depression. If this sounds familiar, or a partner notices pauses in your breathing, ask your GP about a sleep assessment. Treatment can transform energy, mood and concentration.

title: Alcohol and sleep
body: A drink in the evening might help you nod off, but alcohol disrupts sleep later in the night, causing lighter sleep, more waking and more night sweats for some women. Australian guidelines suggest no more than ten standard drinks a week and no more than four on any one day, and less is better. Try a few alcohol-free nights and notice how you sleep.

title: Melatonin
body: Melatonin is a hormone that helps regulate your body clock. In Australia, some low-dose melatonin products are available from pharmacists for adults over 55, and others need a prescription. Its effect on menopausal sleep problems is modest and evidence is limited. Speak with your pharmacist or GP before trying it, especially if you take other medicines. Good sleep habits and CBT for insomnia remain the first-line approaches.

title: Hormone therapy and sleep
body: For women whose sleep is disrupted by night sweats, menopausal hormone therapy can improve sleep by reducing the sweats. Some women also find micronised progesterone taken at night helps them feel sleepy. Whether hormone therapy is right for you depends on your health and history, so it's a conversation to have with your GP. Good sleep habits still help alongside any treatment. If sleep problems continue on MHT, it's worth asking about CBT for insomnia or checking for other causes such as sleep apnoea.

title: Sleep and mood are linked
body: Poor sleep and low mood feed each other. A bad night makes you more irritable, anxious and teary, and stress and worry make it harder to sleep. That's why improving sleep often lifts mood, and why looking after mood helps sleep. Mood Mapper's sleep tags can help you see this link in your own life. Protecting sleep is one of the kindest things you can do for your mood. Even small improvements, like a steadier wake time, can help both.

title: A short body scan
body: Lie comfortably and let your breath slow. Bring attention to your feet and notice how they feel, without changing anything. Slowly move your attention up: legs, hips, belly, chest, hands, arms, shoulders, neck and face. If you notice tension, imagine breathing into that area and letting it soften. If your mind wanders, gently come back. It's practice, not performance. The wind-down area offers guided versions of this.

title: Is brain fog real?
body: Yes. Many women notice forgetfulness, word-finding trouble and poorer concentration in perimenopause. Large research studies have found small but measurable changes in memory and processing speed during the transition. Importantly, these changes appear to be temporary, with performance tending to recover after menopause. Brain fog isn't imagined, and it isn't a sign that something is seriously wrong. Practical strategies, good sleep and managing stress can help while it lasts.

title: Is brain fog dementia?
body: Brain fog in perimenopause is very common and is not an early sign of dementia. Research suggests memory and thinking tend to recover after the menopause transition. Forgetting where you put your keys is different to dementia, which involves progressive problems that affect daily functioning. If you're worried about significant memory changes, see your GP, who can check for other causes like thyroid problems or low iron.

title: What makes brain fog worse
body: Poor sleep, stress, multitasking, low mood, anxiety and alcohol can all make brain fog worse. Low iron, thyroid problems and some medicines can also affect thinking. Many of these can be improved. Protecting sleep, single-tasking when you can, writing things down and regular exercise can make a real difference to how sharp you feel. Your GP can check iron and thyroid levels if fog is persistent or getting worse.

title: Practical strategies for brain fog
body: Give your brain a break by getting things out of your head. Write tasks down, use reminders, give everyday items a fixed home and keep a running list. Do one thing at a time where you can. Tackle demanding tasks when you're freshest. Say a word you've lost aloud with a description; it often comes back. Tools like Side Quest Saver and the Very Important Thing Department are built for this.

title: Word-finding trouble
body: Struggling to find a word mid-sentence is one of the most commonly reported parts of brain fog. It can feel embarrassing, especially at work. Try describing the word instead, pausing calmly, or moving on; the word often pops up later. Remind yourself it's common and temporary. Little word games can be a fun way to keep your vocabulary ticking over.

title: Exercise and your brain
body: Regular physical activity supports brain health, mood and sleep, all of which help thinking. Australian guidelines suggest 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, like brisk walking, plus muscle-strengthening on at least two days. Even a short walk can clear your head. Exercise with others adds social connection, which is also good for the brain. Choose activities you enjoy so you'll keep doing them.

title: Brain fog at work
body: At work, brain fog can shake your confidence. Practical supports include keeping notes in meetings, using calendar reminders, blocking focus time, asking for written follow-ups and building checklists for routine tasks. Many of these help everyone, so they're easy to adopt. If symptoms are affecting your work, you might talk with your manager about flexible adjustments, and with your GP about treatment.

title: Single-tasking
body: Multitasking is harder on a foggy brain. Each switch between tasks costs attention, so you're more likely to lose track. Where you can, do one thing at a time, finish a small chunk, then move on. Close extra tabs on your screen and in your head. The 37 tabs tool is a playful way to practise choosing just one thing.

title: Being kind to your forgetful brain
body: It's easy to be harsh with yourself when you forget things. Self-criticism adds stress, and stress makes memory worse. Try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend: that's annoying, and it's understandable, my brain is carrying a lot right now. A little self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook; it actually makes it easier to cope and problem-solve.

title: Hormone therapy and brain fog
body: Some women feel clearer-headed on menopausal hormone therapy, often because it improves sleep and hot flushes. However, there isn't strong trial evidence that hormone therapy directly treats perimenopausal brain fog, and it isn't recommended specifically to prevent dementia. If brain fog is troubling you, talk with your GP about all the factors involved, including sleep, mood and other health conditions.

title: Depression in perimenopause
body: The risk of depression rises during perimenopause, even for women who have never been depressed before. A 2024 analysis of international studies found women in perimenopause were about 40% more likely to experience depressive symptoms than those before perimenopause. Women with a past history of depression, severe premenstrual symptoms or postnatal depression may be more vulnerable. Depression is treatable, and reaching out is a strong step.

title: Signs it's more than a rough patch
body: Everyone has down days. It may be more than a rough patch if, for two weeks or more, you feel low or flat most of the time, lose interest in things you usually enjoy, feel hopeless or worthless, or notice changes in sleep, appetite and energy. If this sounds like you, please talk with your GP. If you have thoughts of suicide, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 now.

title: Irritability and rage
body: Many women describe a shorter fuse in perimenopause, sometimes surprising rage over small things. Hormone shifts, poor sleep, overload and unmet needs all feed it. Noticing early signs, like tension or a racing heart, and taking a pause before reacting can help. So can sharing the load and protecting sleep. If anger is affecting your relationships, a psychologist can help you with practical strategies.

title: Feeling overwhelmed
body: Overwhelm often comes from too many demands and too little capacity at once, and perimenopause can shrink that capacity through poor sleep and hormonal changes. Try a quick reset: one long breath out, then pick just one next action. Afterwards, look at what can be dropped, delayed or delegated. Asking for help is a skill, not a weakness. The 37 tabs tool can walk you through a quick reset.

title: Anxiety skills you can use anywhere
body: When anxiety rises, try breathing out for longer than you breathe in, which signals safety to your body. Ground yourself with 5-4-3-2-1: name five things you can see, four you can feel, three you can hear, two you can smell and one slow breath. Notice anxious thoughts as thoughts, not facts. Regular exercise and limiting caffeine also help over time.

title: Treatments for mood in perimenopause
body: Support for mood includes lifestyle changes like regular activity, better sleep and less alcohol; psychological therapies such as CBT; and medicines like antidepressants. Many Australian doctors also see mood benefits from menopausal hormone therapy, and there's evidence oestrogen can help depressive symptoms in perimenopause. The right mix depends on you, so talk with your GP about your symptoms and history.

title: Seeing a psychologist through Medicare
body: Your GP can prepare a mental health treatment plan, which lets you claim a Medicare rebate for a set number of sessions with a psychologist each calendar year. Ask your GP how many sessions are currently covered and whether any gap fee applies. The Australian Psychological Society's Find a Psychologist service can help you find someone with experience in women's health.

title: Grief and loss at midlife
body: Midlife can bring loss as well as change: the end of fertility, children leaving home, ageing or unwell parents, shifts in identity and body. Even when menopause is welcome, it's common to feel some grief. Naming these feelings, talking with people you trust and allowing yourself time can help. A psychologist can support you if grief feels heavy or stuck.

title: Who am I now?
body: Many women find perimenopause raises big questions about identity, purpose and what they want for the next chapter. It can feel unsettling, but it's also an invitation to reflect on your values and what matters most. Some women describe this time as the start of greater confidence and freedom. You don't have to have the answers yet; curiosity is a good place to start.

title: Self-compassion
body: Self-compassion means treating yourself with the kindness you'd offer a good friend. It involves noticing you're struggling, remembering others go through this too, and responding with care rather than criticism. Research links self-compassion to lower anxiety and depression and better coping. Try placing a hand on your chest and saying, this is hard right now, and I'm doing my best.

title: Staying connected
body: Connection with others is one of the strongest protectors of mental health. When you're tired or low, it's tempting to withdraw. Try small steps: a walk with a friend, a message to someone who gets it, joining a group or a menopause community. Talking about what you're going through often reveals you're not the only one. Even brief contact counts, and connection is something you can build back up gradually.

title: Mood and your cycle
body: In perimenopause, mood changes may cluster around certain parts of your cycle, especially the days before a period, when hormone swings can be largest. Tracking mood alongside your cycle can reveal this. Knowing a tough patch is likely can help you plan: lighten your load, protect sleep and warn the people around you. It's also useful information for your GP.

title: Past depression and perimenopause
body: If you've had depression before, including postnatal depression, or severe premenstrual mood changes, you may be more sensitive to the hormonal shifts of perimenopause. This doesn't mean depression will return, but it's worth being alert to early signs and having a plan. Let your GP know your history so you can catch changes early and get support quickly. Mood Mapper can help you notice early changes.

title: Small things that lift mood
body: Some evidence-based mood boosters: get outside in daylight, move your body, do something you enjoy even briefly, connect with someone, help someone else, finish a small task, and limit alcohol. On flat days, start smaller than you think you need to. Action often comes before motivation, not after. A little win can be the first step. Pick one and do it for five minutes; that's enough to start.

title: Thoughts of suicide
body: If you're having thoughts of ending your life, please reach out now. Call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, any time. If you're in immediate danger, call 000. You can also contact the Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467 or speak to your GP. You deserve support, and these feelings can change with the right help.

title: Mindfulness
body: Mindfulness means paying attention to the present moment with curiosity instead of judgement. It can help with stress, worry and coping with symptoms like hot flushes, even if it doesn't stop them. Start small: one minute noticing your breath, or fully tasting a cup of tea. When your mind wanders, gently come back. It's a skill that grows with practice.

title: Asking for help
body: Asking for help can feel hard, especially if you're used to being the one who holds everything together. But you don't have to manage perimenopause alone. Help might mean telling your partner what you need, asking family to share the load, talking to your manager or booking a GP appointment. Reaching out is a sign of strength and self-respect. Start with one small, specific request.

title: What is MHT?
body: Menopausal hormone therapy, or MHT, replaces some of the hormones your body makes less of around menopause, mainly oestrogen. It's the same thing many people call HRT, hormone replacement therapy. Australian experts now prefer the term MHT. It's the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats and also helps vaginal dryness, sleep and, for many women, mood. Whether it suits you depends on your health and history.

title: MHT or HRT: what's the difference?
body: There's no difference in the treatment. HRT, hormone replacement therapy, is the older and more familiar name. MHT, menopausal hormone therapy, is the term Australian menopause specialists now prefer, because the aim is to relieve symptoms and protect health rather than to replace hormones to younger levels. You'll see both terms used, and Sprout uses MHT. Whichever name your doctor uses, the medicines and the conversation are the same.

title: How MHT works
body: MHT supplies oestrogen to ease symptoms caused by falling oestrogen, such as hot flushes, night sweats and vaginal dryness. If you still have a uterus, a progestogen is added to protect the lining of the womb, because oestrogen on its own would increase the risk of uterine cancer. Doctors generally start low, go slow and review regularly to find the dose that controls symptoms.

title: Who might consider MHT?
body: MHT is most often considered for women with menopausal symptoms that affect their quality of life, such as hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disruption or mood changes. Australian guidance says that for healthy women around the usual age of menopause, the benefits generally outweigh the risks. It's also usually recommended for women with early or premature menopause. Your GP will consider your symptoms, age, history and preferences.

title: Who may not be able to use MHT
body: MHT may not be suitable if you have had breast cancer or another hormone-sensitive cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, a past blood clot in a vein or lungs, a stroke or heart disease, active liver disease or uncontrolled high blood pressure. Some of these situations may still allow certain forms with specialist advice. Your doctor will go through your history carefully, and non-hormonal options are available.

title: The timing of MHT
body: International and Australian experts agree that for most healthy women with symptoms, starting MHT under 60 or within ten years of menopause has the most favourable balance of benefits and risks. Starting much later can carry more risk, especially for heart disease and stroke. That doesn't mean it's too late to talk about options; your doctor can weigh things up for your situation.

title: How long can you take MHT?
body: There's no single fixed time limit. Current international guidance says MHT doesn't need to be routinely stopped at a particular age, such as 60 or 65. Instead, you and your doctor review each year whether the benefits still outweigh the risks for you. Some women use it for a few years, others longer, for example for ongoing symptoms or bone protection.

title: Starting MHT: what to expect
body: When you start MHT, symptoms often improve within a few weeks, though it can take up to three months to feel the full effect. Early side effects like breast tenderness, bloating, nausea, headaches or irregular bleeding are common and often settle within a few months. Your doctor will usually review you after about three to six months, then regularly. Keep a note of how you feel.

title: Common early side effects
body: Common early side effects of MHT include breast tenderness, bloating, fluid retention, nausea, headaches, leg cramps and irregular bleeding or spotting. They often ease within the first few months as your body adjusts. If they don't, your doctor may adjust the dose, type or way you take it. Don't stop suddenly without talking to your doctor, and report anything that worries you.

title: Bleeding on MHT
body: Bleeding patterns depend on the type of MHT. Cyclical regimens usually cause a regular, period-like bleed each month. Continuous combined regimens often cause irregular spotting for the first few months, which usually settles. Persistent bleeding after the first six months on continuous therapy, or any unexpected heavy bleeding, should be checked by your doctor. Tracking bleeding in Cycle Tracker helps you report it accurately.

title: Does MHT cause weight gain?
body: No. Research shows women using MHT don't gain more weight than women who don't. Midlife weight gain is mainly linked to ageing, reduced muscle mass, lifestyle and life circumstances. Menopause does shift where fat is stored, toward the tummy. Some women notice bloating or fluid retention when starting MHT, which usually settles. Strength training, activity and good sleep help most.

title: Stopping MHT
body: When you stop MHT, symptoms like hot flushes may return for some women, but not all. Research suggests stopping gradually or suddenly makes little difference to whether symptoms come back in the long run, though some women prefer to taper. It's best to plan stopping with your doctor, who can help you decide when and how, and what to do if symptoms return.

title: Is MHT a contraceptive?
body: No. MHT doesn't contain enough hormone to prevent pregnancy. If you're in perimenopause and want to avoid pregnancy, you'll still need contraception, generally until two years after your last period if you're under 50, or one year if you're over 50. One option, the levonorgestrel intrauterine device, can provide both contraception and the progestogen part of MHT. Your GP can help you plan both together.

title: MHT cost and the PBS
body: Many forms of MHT are subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, which caps what you pay per prescription. In March 2025 several more body-identical options, including an oestradiol gel and micronised progesterone, were added to the PBS, making them much more affordable. Some products remain private prescriptions. Ask your GP or pharmacist about the cost of the options you're considering.

title: Reviewing your MHT each year
body: Experts recommend reviewing MHT at least once a year with your doctor. It's a chance to check how symptoms are going, any side effects or bleeding, your blood pressure, breast screening and overall health, and whether the dose or type still suits you. It's also a good time to talk about how long to continue. Bring your Medicine Cabinet history to the appointment.

title: Questions to ask about MHT
body: Useful questions for your GP include: Is MHT a reasonable option for me? Which type and form would suit me and why? What benefits and risks apply to my health history? How soon should I notice a difference? What side effects or bleeding should I expect? When should we review it? What are my non-hormonal options? Writing questions down beforehand helps you remember them.

title: MHT for perimenopause
body: MHT can be used in perimenopause, while you're still having periods, not just after menopause. Treatment is often adjusted for perimenopause, for example using cyclical progestogen so bleeding stays predictable, or using a hormonal intrauterine device as the progestogen part. Because hormone levels still fluctuate, finding the right approach can take some adjustment. A GP with menopause experience can help.

title: Mood benefits of MHT
body: Some international guidelines don't list MHT as a first-line treatment for depression, but many Australian doctors observe mood benefits in perimenopause, and studies suggest oestrogen can have antidepressant effects during this time. MHT can also improve mood indirectly by reducing night sweats and improving sleep. If mood is a major concern, discuss all options with your GP, including psychological therapy and antidepressants.

title: Finding a doctor experienced in menopause
body: Most women can get good menopause care from their GP. If you'd like someone with extra expertise, the Australasian Menopause Society has a Find an AMS Doctor service listing GPs and specialists with a special interest in menopause. Some hospitals also run menopause clinics, and some endometriosis and pelvic pain clinics now include menopause support. Your GP can refer you if needed.

title: Oestrogen-only MHT
body: Oestrogen-only MHT is used by women who've had a hysterectomy and no longer have a uterus. Because there's no womb lining to protect, a progestogen isn't needed. Research shows oestrogen-only therapy has a lower breast cancer risk than combined therapy, with little or no increase for many women. It can be taken as tablets, patches, gels or sprays, depending on what suits you.

title: Combined MHT
body: Combined MHT contains both an oestrogen and a progestogen, and is used by women who still have a uterus. The progestogen protects the lining of the womb from overgrowth, which reduces the risk of uterine cancer. Combined MHT can be taken as separate products, such as a gel and a capsule, or as combined tablets or patches. It can be taken cyclically or continuously.

title: Cyclical versus continuous MHT
body: With cyclical, or sequential, MHT you take oestrogen every day and a progestogen for part of each month, often 12 to 14 days, which usually leads to a monthly bleed. It's often used in perimenopause or soon after menopause. With continuous combined MHT you take both every day, aiming for no bleeding after an initial settling period. It's usually used once you're postmenopausal.

title: Oestrogen tablets
body: Oestrogen can be taken as a daily tablet. Tablets are effective and familiar, but because oral oestrogen passes through the liver, it slightly increases the risk of blood clots, roughly doubling a low baseline risk. For women with a higher clot risk, migraines or certain other conditions, doctors may suggest a patch, gel or spray instead. Many women use tablets safely.

title: Oestrogen patches
body: Oestrogen patches stick to the skin, usually on the lower tummy or buttock, and slowly release oestradiol. Most are changed twice a week. Because oestrogen through the skin bypasses the liver, patches appear to carry minimal or no increased risk of blood clots. Rotate where you place each patch to avoid skin irritation, and avoid putting them on the breasts. Medicine Cabinet can track your patch days.

title: Oestrogen gel
body: Oestrogen gel is rubbed into the skin each day, usually on the arms or thighs, as directed. Like patches, gel delivers oestradiol through the skin, so it appears to carry minimal or no increased clot risk. Doses are measured in pumps or sachets. Let it dry before dressing, and avoid skin contact with others until it's absorbed. In 2025 an oestradiol gel was added to the PBS.

title: Oestrogen spray
body: Some oestradiol is available as a skin spray, usually applied to the inner forearm. Like patches and gels, sprays deliver oestrogen through the skin. They can be a convenient option for women who find gels messy or patches irritating. As with gels, let the spray dry before covering the area, and avoid skin-to-skin contact with children and pets until it has absorbed.

title: Body-identical hormones
body: Body-identical hormones have the same chemical structure as the hormones your body makes. In Australia, regulated body-identical options include oestradiol in tablets, patches, gels and sprays, and micronised progesterone capsules. These are tested, quality-controlled and approved by the TGA. They're different from compounded bioidentical hormones, which aren't regulated and aren't recommended by the Australasian Menopause Society. Many are subsidised on the PBS.

title: Micronised progesterone
body: Micronised progesterone is a body-identical progesterone taken as a capsule, usually at night because it can make you drowsy. It's used with oestrogen to protect the womb lining. Depending on the regimen, it may be taken on 12 days of each 28-day cycle or on most days continuously. It was added to the PBS in March 2025, and a combined gel-and-capsule pack is also available.

title: Progestogens explained
body: Progestogen is the umbrella term for progesterone and its synthetic relatives, called progestins. In MHT they protect the womb lining. Options include micronised progesterone, dydrogesterone, norethisterone, medroxyprogesterone, drospirenone and levonorgestrel.
