They differ in side effects and possibly in breast cancer risk; some evidence suggests micronised progesterone and dydrogesterone may carry lower risk. Your doctor can help choose one that suits you.

title: The hormonal IUD in MHT
body: A levonorgestrel intrauterine device, or hormonal IUD, releases a progestogen directly into the womb. It can provide the progestogen part of combined MHT, so you only need to add oestrogen. It also provides contraception and can make periods much lighter, which suits many women in perimenopause. When used for womb protection with MHT, it's generally replaced after five years. Your GP or gynaecologist can discuss insertion.

title: Combined patches and tablets
body: Some MHT products combine oestrogen and a progestogen in a single patch or tablet, which can make treatment simpler. Combined patches are usually changed twice a week. Combined tablets come in cyclical packs, which cause a monthly bleed, or continuous packs, which aim for no bleeding. A combined capsule containing both oestradiol and progesterone is also available. Your doctor can explain what suits your stage.

title: Tibolone
body: Tibolone is a daily tablet with effects similar to oestrogen, progesterone and testosterone combined. It's used by postmenopausal women and can help hot flushes, sexual function and bone protection. It's generally not suitable in perimenopause because it can cause irregular bleeding, and it's not suitable after breast cancer. It may carry a higher stroke risk if started after age 60.

title: Oestrogen with bazedoxifene
body: One tablet option combines conjugated oestrogens with bazedoxifene, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator. The bazedoxifene protects the womb lining instead of a progestogen. It helps hot flushes and night sweats and helps prevent bone loss, and tends to cause less breast tenderness and bleeding than some other options. It's only suitable for women who still have a uterus. Your doctor can explain whether it suits your situation.

title: Choosing a form that suits you
body: The best form of MHT depends on your health, preferences and lifestyle. Patches suit people who prefer not to think about it daily. Gels and sprays allow flexible dosing. Tablets are simple and familiar. A hormonal IUD can cover contraception and womb protection at once. Clot risk, migraines, skin sensitivity and cost all play a part. It's fine to try another form if one doesn't suit you.

title: Applying gel and patches well
body: For gels, apply to clean, dry skin as directed, let it dry before dressing, wash your hands and avoid others touching the area until absorbed. For patches, press firmly for about ten seconds on clean, dry, hair-free skin, change on the same days each week, rotate sites and fold used patches in half before disposing. Medicine Cabinet can remind you and track patch sites.

title: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen
body: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen comes as a cream, pessary or tablet inserted into the vagina. It treats local symptoms like dryness, irritation, painful sex and recurrent urinary infections. Very little is absorbed into the bloodstream, so it doesn't need a progestogen and can generally be used long-term. A common pattern is daily for about two weeks, then twice weekly, though your doctor will advise.

title: Vaginal DHEA (prasterone)
body: Prasterone is a vaginal insert containing DHEA, a hormone that the vaginal tissues convert locally into oestrogen and androgens. It's approved in Australia for moderate to severe vaginal symptoms after menopause. It's used daily. It's an option if vaginal oestrogen doesn't suit you, though evidence after breast cancer is limited and specialist advice is needed in that situation. Your GP can discuss whether it suits you.

title: Compounded bioidentical hormones
body: Compounded bioidentical hormones are made up individually by some pharmacies, often as creams, lozenges or troches, and dosed using saliva tests. The Australasian Menopause Society doesn't recommend them. They're not tested for quality, safety or effectiveness, doses can be inconsistent, and some have been linked to uterine cancer when the progesterone didn't protect the womb. Regulated body-identical options are available instead.

title: MHT forms and schedules at a glance
body: Common MHT schedules include: oestrogen gel or tablets every day; patches changed twice a week; progesterone capsules on 12 days of every 28, or on most days; combined tablets every day; vaginal oestrogen daily for two weeks then twice weekly; and a hormonal IUD replaced every five years when used with MHT. Always follow your own prescription. Medicine Cabinet handles all of these patterns.

title: Benefits of MHT
body: MHT is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. It also improves vaginal dryness and discomfort, often improves sleep and, for many women, mood, joint aches and quality of life. It helps prevent bone loss and reduces the risk of fractures. Starting MHT within ten years of menopause may also have heart benefits for some women. Benefits depend on your situation.

title: MHT and breast cancer: the big picture
body: Combined MHT is linked to a small increase in breast cancer risk, which grows with longer use and falls again after stopping. Oestrogen-only MHT shows little or no increase. To keep this in perspective, other factors like alcohol and higher body weight after menopause carry similar or larger risks. Your personal risk depends on your history, so talk it through with your doctor.

title: Understanding breast cancer numbers
body: Early reports from a large US study were widely misread, causing fear that many women on MHT would get breast cancer. In fact, that study found no increased risk with up to five years of combined MHT in women starting in their 50s, and only a small increase after longer follow-up, of around nine extra cases per 10,000 women. Oestrogen alone showed no increase.

title: MHT and blood clots
body: Oestrogen tablets roughly double the risk of a blood clot in a vein, though because the starting risk is low, this means about one extra case per 1,000 women. Oestrogen through the skin, as patches, gels or sprays, appears to carry minimal or no increased risk. If you've had a clot or have a higher risk, your doctor may suggest a skin-based form or another option.

title: MHT and heart health
body: When MHT is started under 60 or within ten years of menopause, research shows no increase in heart disease, and oestrogen-only therapy may even lower risk. Starting much later, or with existing heart disease, is different and needs careful assessment. MHT isn't prescribed purely to prevent heart disease. A healthy lifestyle and managing blood pressure and cholesterol remain the foundation of heart health.

title: MHT and stroke
body: For healthy women in their 50s or within ten years of menopause, the risk of stroke from MHT appears very low. Risk is higher with tablets and higher doses, and in older women starting MHT later. Skin-based forms may be safer for women with stroke risk factors. Your doctor will consider your blood pressure, migraines, smoking and other factors when discussing options.

title: MHT and uterine cancer
body: Taking oestrogen alone when you have a uterus increases the risk of uterine (endometrial) cancer, because oestrogen thickens the womb lining. That's why women with a uterus take a progestogen too, which protects the lining. It's important to take the progestogen as prescribed. Any unexpected or persistent bleeding on MHT should be checked by your doctor. Tracking bleeding in Cycle Tracker helps you report patterns accurately.

title: MHT and bone health
body: Oestrogen helps keep bones strong, and bone loss speeds up around menopause. MHT helps prevent this bone loss and reduces the risk of fractures, including hip and spine fractures. For women with early menopause, MHT is especially important for bone protection until at least the average age of menopause. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D support bones too. Your GP can assess your bone health risk.

title: MHT and migraine
body: Women with migraine can often use MHT, but the type matters. Skin-based oestrogen, like patches or gel, is usually preferred because it gives steadier hormone levels and may carry less stroke risk than tablets, particularly for migraine with aura. Some women find migraines improve on steady MHT; others notice changes. Keeping a headache diary helps your doctor fine-tune treatment. Always mention migraine history when discussing MHT.

title: MHT after breast cancer
body: MHT is generally not recommended after breast cancer, because many breast cancers are sensitive to hormones. For vaginal symptoms, non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants are tried first; if symptoms persist, low-dose vaginal oestrogen may be considered after discussing with your oncologist. For hot flushes, non-hormonal medicines, CBT and hypnosis can help. Your cancer team and GP can guide you. Each situation is individual.

title: MHT and family history of breast cancer
body: Having a family history of breast cancer doesn't automatically rule out MHT. Your doctor will consider how close the relatives were, their ages at diagnosis and any known gene changes, alongside your symptoms and other risks. Some women may be referred to a family cancer clinic. It's a personal decision worth discussing carefully rather than assuming the answer is no.

title: MHT and endometriosis
body: Women with a history of endometriosis can often use MHT, but specialists usually recommend combined therapy, even after hysterectomy, to reduce the chance of endometriosis returning. The decision depends on your history and surgery. Talk with your GP or gynaecologist about the safest option for you. The type, dose and timing of MHT may be tailored, and your specialist can explain what's likely to suit you. Keeping track of any pelvic pain or bleeding changes helps them adjust treatment over time.

title: Weighing up MHT
body: Deciding about MHT is a personal choice based on how much symptoms affect you, your health history, your preferences and the evidence. For many healthy women around the usual age of menopause, benefits outweigh risks. For others, non-hormonal options may be better. There's no right or wrong answer, only the right answer for you, made with good information and a doctor you trust.

title: MHT myths at a glance
body: Some common myths: that MHT causes weight gain (it doesn't); that a quarter of women on MHT get breast cancer (they don't; the risk is small); that MHT causes heart disease when started at the usual age (research shows no increase); that you need blood tests to start (usually not); and that compounded hormones are safer (they're not regulated and aren't recommended).

title: Mammograms and MHT
body: Women using MHT should keep up with regular breast screening. BreastScreen Australia offers free mammograms every two years for women aged 50 to 74, and women from 40 can also attend. MHT can increase breast density for some women, which can make mammograms a little harder to read. Let the screening service know you're using MHT, and report any breast changes promptly.

title: MHT for early menopause
body: For women with menopause before 45, and especially before 40, MHT is usually recommended until at least the average age of menopause, around 51, unless there's a reason not to use it. This replaces hormones the body would normally still be making and helps protect bones, heart and brain. The usual breast cancer risk information for older women doesn't apply in the same way.

title: Testosterone for women
body: In Australia, a 1% testosterone cream is approved for postmenopausal women with low sexual desire that causes distress, after other factors have been addressed. It isn't approved for energy, mood, brain fog or bone health, and evidence doesn't support those uses. Doctors check blood levels before and during treatment and usually stop if there's no benefit by six months. Male products and compounded preparations shouldn't be used.

title: Testosterone side effects and cautions
body: Testosterone side effects in women can include acne and increased hair growth, which usually signal the dose is too high. Rarely, effects like voice deepening or clitoral enlargement can be permanent. It isn't suitable with hormone-sensitive cancers, existing acne or excess hair, and professional singers are advised to avoid it. Long-term safety data beyond about two years are limited, so regular review is important.

title: Hormones and libido
body: Research shows declining sexual function at menopause tracks more with falling oestrogen than with testosterone, and testosterone levels don't drop sharply in natural menopause. So optimising oestrogen, including treating vaginal dryness, is usually the first step. Surgical removal of the ovaries does lower testosterone substantially. Relationship, mood, fatigue and medicine factors matter too, which is why a whole-person approach works best.

title: Contraception choices in perimenopause
body: Contraception options in perimenopause include the hormonal IUD, copper IUD, contraceptive implant, progestogen-only pill and barrier methods. The hormonal IUD can also lighten heavy periods and be used as the progestogen part of MHT. Combined pills and rings are generally not recommended after 50. Fertility awareness methods are unreliable with irregular cycles. Your GP can help you find what fits your health and plans.

title: When can I stop contraception?
body: Australian guidance generally suggests continuing contraception until you've had two years without a period if you're under 50, or one year without a period if you're over 50. If you're using hormonal contraception that stops periods, it's harder to tell when menopause has happened, so your doctor may suggest a blood test or simply continuing until around 55, when natural fertility has almost always ended.

title: Treating heavy periods
body: Heavy periods in perimenopause can often be treated. Options include the hormonal IUD, which can greatly reduce bleeding, tranexamic acid or anti-inflammatory medicines taken during periods, and some hormonal tablets. Your GP may check your iron levels and arrange an ultrasound to look for causes like fibroids or polyps. Don't put up with flooding; it's common, but it's treatable. Tracking flow helps your GP gauge severity.

title: The pill in perimenopause
body: For some women under 50 without risk factors, a combined contraceptive pill can manage perimenopausal symptoms, regulate bleeding and provide contraception all at once. It isn't suitable for women who smoke over 35, have migraines with aura, high blood pressure or a history of clots, and it's generally not recommended after 50. Your GP can advise whether it's an option for you.

title: Non-hormonal options overview
body: If you can't or prefer not to use hormones, there are effective options. Prescription choices include newer medicines that target the brain's temperature centre, certain low-dose antidepressants, gabapentin, and some other medicines. Psychological approaches like CBT and clinical hypnosis have good evidence. Non-hormonal options are generally less effective than MHT for hot flushes, but they help many women. Your GP can talk through what suits you.

title: Fezolinetant
body: Fezolinetant is a non-hormonal tablet approved by the TGA in 2024 for moderate to severe hot flushes and night sweats. It works by blocking a signal, called neurokinin B, in the brain's temperature control centre. It's taken once a day. Because liver problems have been reported, doctors check liver blood tests before and during treatment. Ask your GP about suitability and cost.

title: Elinzanetant
body: Elinzanetant is a newer non-hormonal medicine that has also been approved in Australia for menopausal hot flushes. Like fezolinetant, it acts on neurokinin signalling in the brain's temperature centre, and it may also help sleep disrupted by night sweats. As a newer medicine, long-term experience is still growing. Your GP or specialist can discuss whether it's suitable and what it would cost.

title: Antidepressants for hot flushes
body: Some antidepressants, used at low doses, can reduce hot flushes and night sweats, including venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, escitalopram and paroxetine. Some types help around 70% of women with more severe symptoms. They can also help mood and anxiety. Side effects may include nausea, dry mouth or changes in sleep or sexual function. Paroxetine may interact with tamoxifen, so tell your doctor about all your medicines.

title: Gabapentin
body: Gabapentin, a medicine originally used for epilepsy and nerve pain, can reduce hot flushes and night sweats and may be particularly useful when night sweats disturb sleep, as it's often taken at night. Side effects can include drowsiness and dizziness, especially at first. It's prescribed off-label for this use, and your GP can discuss whether it suits you. Tell your doctor about all your medicines.

title: Clonidine and oxybutynin
body: Clonidine, a blood pressure medicine, has been used for decades and may help some women with milder hot flushes, though benefits are modest. Oxybutynin, a bladder medicine, can also reduce hot flushes, but long-term use is linked to cognitive side effects in older people, so it's used cautiously. These are options your GP may mention if others don't suit. Always discuss side effects and other medicines first.

title: Psychological treatments
body: Cognitive behavioural therapy and clinical hypnosis are both recommended by international menopause experts for hot flushes. CBT also helps sleep, low mood, anxiety and coping with symptoms. These approaches teach skills you keep using, and they suit women who can't or prefer not to take medicines. Your GP can refer you to a psychologist, and some programs are delivered online or in groups.

title: Weight and hot flushes
body: Research suggests carrying extra weight can make hot flushes worse, and that weight loss may reduce them for some women, especially early in the transition. If weight is a concern for you, small sustainable changes in activity, eating and sleep work better than strict diets. Focus on strength and wellbeing rather than the number on the scale, and be kind to yourself along the way.

title: Stellate ganglion block
body: A stellate ganglion block is an injection of local anaesthetic near nerves at the base of the neck. Some studies suggest it can reduce moderate to severe hot flushes. It's considered an emerging option in Australia, not widely available and usually offered only in specialist settings. Ask a menopause specialist if you're interested and other options haven't helped. Long-term evidence is still developing.

title: Treatments without good evidence
body: International menopause experts have found that paced breathing, yoga, exercise, cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, diet changes, acupuncture and most supplements don't reliably reduce hot flushes themselves. That doesn't mean they're useless; many improve wellbeing, sleep and comfort, and some women find them helpful. It just means they're not proven treatments for hot flushes, so don't feel you've failed if they don't stop them.

title: Are natural therapies safe?
body: Natural doesn't automatically mean safe or effective. Some herbal and complementary products can interact with prescription medicines, affect bleeding or be unsuitable with certain conditions. Quality and purity can vary, especially for products bought online. If you're considering a natural therapy, check with your GP or pharmacist first, and tell them about everything you take. Bring the product packaging along so they can check the ingredients.

title: Black cohosh
body: Black cohosh is one of the most popular herbal remedies for hot flushes, but research results are inconsistent and it hasn't been shown to work reliably. Rare cases of liver problems have been reported. If you try it, choose a reputable product, tell your doctor and stop if you notice symptoms like yellowing skin, dark urine or tummy pain. Ask your pharmacist about interactions too.

title: Soy and isoflavones
body: Soy foods and isoflavone supplements contain plant compounds with weak oestrogen-like effects. Studies show inconsistent results, with at most a modest effect on hot flushes for some women. Soy as part of a normal diet is generally fine, but the Australasian Menopause Society advises avoiding soy supplements if you can't take MHT for safety reasons, such as a hormone-sensitive cancer.

title: Supplements bought online
body: Supplements marketed for menopause are a big industry, and claims often outstrip evidence. Products bought online from overseas may not meet Australian standards and can contain undeclared ingredients. In Australia, look for an AUST L or AUST R number on the label. Before spending money, ask your pharmacist what the evidence shows and whether it's safe with your other medicines.

title: Acupuncture
body: Some women find acupuncture relaxing and feel it helps their wellbeing, but research hasn't shown it reliably reduces hot flushes compared with sham treatment. If you choose acupuncture, see a registered practitioner. It's best seen as a wellbeing option rather than a treatment for menopausal symptoms. It shouldn't replace treatments with stronger evidence if your symptoms are severe. Some women enjoy it as part of a broader approach to relaxation and self-care, and that's a perfectly reasonable choice.

title: Yoga and relaxation
body: Yoga, relaxation and mindfulness may not stop hot flushes, but some studies suggest yoga can improve sleep and overall menopausal symptoms and wellbeing. Gentle movement, stretching and breathing can also ease stress and joint stiffness. If you enjoy them, they're a great addition to your week. Wind-down in Pause and Play offers short relaxation practices you can use anytime. Choose a style that feels good for your body.

title: Magnesium and other sleep supplements
body: Magnesium, valerian and other supplements are often promoted for sleep and menopause. Evidence for menopausal symptoms is limited or mixed. Magnesium is generally safe in usual doses for most people but can interact with some medicines and cause tummy upset. Good sleep habits and CBT for insomnia have stronger evidence. Check with your pharmacist before adding supplements. Bring a list of all your supplements to appointments.

title: Vitamin D and calcium supplements
body: Calcium and vitamin D are important for bone health after menopause. Most Australian women over 50 need about 1,300 mg of calcium a day, ideally from food such as dairy, calcium-fortified alternatives, tinned fish with bones and leafy greens. Vitamin D comes mainly from safe sun exposure. Your GP can advise whether you need supplements based on your diet, sun exposure and blood tests.

title: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause
body: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM, is the name for vaginal, vulval and urinary changes caused by low oestrogen. Symptoms include dryness, itching, burning, painful sex, needing to pass urine often, urgency and repeated urinary infections. It affects around half of women aged 50 to 60 and more over time, and unlike hot flushes it usually doesn't improve on its own. It's common, under-recognised and very treatable.

title: Vaginal moisturisers and lubricants
body: Vaginal moisturisers are used regularly, often one to three times a week, to keep tissues comfortable. Lubricants are used during sex to reduce friction and pain. Silicone lubricants last longer than water-based ones, and oil-based lubricants can damage latex condoms. Choose fragrance-free products and avoid perfumed washes, which can irritate. These are available without a prescription from pharmacies. Your pharmacist can help you choose a suitable product.

title: Is vaginal oestrogen safe long-term?
body: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen acts mainly on local tissues, with very little absorbed into the bloodstream. International guidance says it can be used at any age and long-term, and it doesn't need a progestogen. It can take up to eight weeks for the full effect. For women with a history of breast cancer, it may still be considered after discussion with the cancer team.

title: Recurrent urinary tract infections
body: After menopause, changes to the vaginal and urinary tissues can make urinary tract infections more frequent. Vaginal oestrogen can reduce the risk of repeat infections. Drinking enough water and not delaying going to the toilet also help. See your GP promptly for burning, stinging, cloudy urine or fever, and especially if infections keep coming back. Your GP can test your urine and discuss prevention options.

title: Bladder leaks
body: Urinary incontinence affects many women in midlife. Stress incontinence is leaking with coughing, sneezing or exercise; urge incontinence is a sudden need to go. Both are common but not a normal part of ageing you have to accept. Pelvic floor training with a physiotherapist helps many women, and other treatments are available. The National Continence Helpline, 1800 33 00 66, offers free, private advice from specialist nurses.

title: Pelvic floor exercises
body: Your pelvic floor muscles support your bladder, bowel and uterus. Strengthening them can improve bladder control, support sexual comfort and reduce prolapse symptoms. Many women do these exercises incorrectly, so a session with a pelvic health physiotherapist is worth it. Once you've learned the technique, short daily practice makes a difference. The Continence Foundation's Pelvic Floor First resources are a good starting point.

title: Painful sex
body: Painful sex at menopause is often caused by vaginal dryness and thinner tissues, and it's very treatable. Lubricants, regular moisturisers and low-dose vaginal oestrogen help most women. Pelvic floor muscle tension can also contribute, which a pelvic health physiotherapist can address. Pain shouldn't be something you push through. Talk with your GP, and with your partner, about what's happening. Most women find real relief with the right approach.

title: Talking about sex with your doctor
body: Many women feel awkward raising sexual concerns, and doctors don't always ask. It can help to write down what's happening and simply say, I'd like to talk about some changes in my sex life. GPs hear these concerns often. Treatments for dryness, pain and low desire are available, and a psychologist with expertise in sexual health can also help. You deserve comfort and pleasure at every age.

title: Intimacy beyond intercourse
body: When desire, comfort or energy change, it can help to widen the idea of intimacy. Touch, massage, affection, time together and honest conversation all build closeness. Taking intercourse off the table for a while can relieve pressure for both partners. Exploring what feels good now, rather than what used to, is a positive step many couples find brings them closer.

title: Vaginal laser therapy
body: Vaginal laser treatments are promoted for vaginal dryness and bladder symptoms, but high-quality trials haven't shown them to work better than a sham treatment, and they can be expensive. Australian experts say there isn't enough evidence to recommend them outside research. Proven treatments like moisturisers, lubricants and vaginal oestrogen are the first options to consider. Ask your GP about evidence-based options first.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Why bones change at menopause
body: Oestrogen helps keep bones strong. When oestrogen drops around menopause, bone loss speeds up, and women can lose bone density quickly in the first years after menopause. Over time this can lead to osteoporosis, where bones become fragile and break more easily. The good news is that exercise, nutrition, not smoking and, where appropriate, treatment can protect your bones. Building strength now helps for decades.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Exercise for strong bones
body: Bones respond to load. Weight-bearing exercise, like brisk walking, jogging, stair climbing and dancing, and progressive resistance training, like lifting weights or using resistance bands, help maintain bone strength. Balance exercises reduce the risk of falls. Aim for muscle-strengthening at least two days a week. If you have osteoporosis or haven't exercised in a while, an exercise physiologist can tailor a safe program.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Calcium for bones
body: Most Australian women over 50 need around 1,300 mg of calcium a day, which is about four serves of dairy or calcium-fortified alternatives. Other sources include tinned fish with soft bones, almonds, tofu set with calcium and leafy greens. Food is the preferred source. If you can't get enough from your diet, your GP or pharmacist can advise on supplements.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Vitamin D and sunshine
body: Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium. Most Australians get it from sunlight. When the UV index is 3 or above, a few minutes of sun on your arms and hands mid-morning or mid-afternoon on most days is usually enough; use sun protection for longer. When UV is below 3, aim for a few hours of midday sun a week. Your GP can check your levels.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Bone density scans
body: A bone density scan, or DXA scan, measures bone strength and helps assess osteoporosis risk. Medicare covers scans for some women, such as those over 70, or with risk factors like early menopause, previous fractures or certain medicines and conditions. Your GP can assess your risk and arrange a scan if appropriate. The menopause health assessment is a good time to ask.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Preventing falls
body: Falls are a major cause of fractures as we age. Strength and balance exercises, good lighting, removing trip hazards at home, wearing supportive shoes and getting your eyesight checked all reduce your risk. Some medicines can affect balance, so ask your pharmacist to review them. Building strength in your 40s and 50s pays off for decades. It's never too late to start balance training.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Heart health after menopause
body: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death for Australian women, causing more deaths than breast cancer. After menopause, changes in cholesterol, blood pressure and fat distribution can raise risk. Women with early menopause have higher risk. A Heart Health Check with your GP is recommended from age 45. Knowing your numbers and acting early makes a real difference.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Know your numbers
body: Midlife is a great time to know your numbers: blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and waist measurement. These help assess your risk of heart disease, stroke and diabetes, which rises after menopause. Your GP can check them in a Heart Health Check or menopause health assessment. Small, steady changes in activity, eating, alcohol and smoking can improve them. Write your results down so you can track them over time.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Physical activity guidelines
body: Australian guidelines recommend adults be active most days, aiming for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity, like brisk walking, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity each week, plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days. Breaking up long periods of sitting also helps. Any movement is better than none, so start where you are and build gradually.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Strength training at midlife
body: Strength training becomes more important at midlife because muscle naturally declines with age and changing hormones. Building muscle supports metabolism, blood sugar, bones, balance, joints and confidence. You don't need a gym; body-weight exercises, resistance bands or carrying shopping all count. Start light, focus on good form and progress gradually. Two sessions a week is a great goal. An exercise physiologist can help you get started safely.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Eating well at midlife
body: A healthy eating pattern helps energy, mood, weight, heart and bone health. Focus on vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, legumes, nuts, fish and enough protein spread across the day, which helps maintain muscle. Include calcium-rich foods. Limit highly processed foods, added sugar and alcohol. There's no special menopause diet; the Australian Dietary Guidelines are a solid foundation. An accredited dietitian can personalise advice.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Protein and muscle
body: Getting enough protein, spread across meals, helps maintain muscle as you age, especially when combined with strength training. Good sources include fish, eggs, lean meat, dairy, legumes, tofu and nuts. Many women find adding protein at breakfast helps energy and fullness. If you have kidney disease or other health conditions, check with your GP or a dietitian first. Pairing protein with strength training works best.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Alcohol at midlife
body: Alcohol can trigger hot flushes, disrupt sleep, affect mood and increase the risk of breast cancer and other conditions. Australian guidelines recommend no more than ten standard drinks a week and no more than four on any one day to reduce health risks, and less is better. Many women find cutting back improves sleep and flushes noticeably. Try a few alcohol-free days each week.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Smoking and menopause
body: Smoking is linked to more hot flushes, earlier menopause, bone loss and higher risk of heart disease, stroke and many cancers. Quitting at any age brings real benefits. Quitline, 13 7848, offers free support, and your GP or pharmacist can help with nicotine replacement and other aids. It's never too late to stop. Quitting can also reduce how often and how strongly hot flushes occur for some women, and it protects your bones and heart for the decades ahead.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Diabetes risk at midlife
body: The risk of type 2 diabetes rises in midlife, and changes in body composition around menopause can affect blood sugar. Regular activity, strength training, a healthy eating pattern and good sleep all help. Your GP can check your blood sugar during a health check. Some research suggests MHT may reduce diabetes risk, but it isn't prescribed for that reason. Small daily habits add up.

category: Body health: bones, heart and movement
title: Cancer screening at midlife
body: Midlife is a good time to check you're up to date with screening. BreastScreen offers free mammograms every two years for women aged 50 to 74. Cervical screening tests are due every five years from 25 to 74. Free bowel cancer screening kits are posted every two years from age 45 to 74 on request or automatically from 50. Ask your GP if you're unsure what's due.

title: Early and premature menopause
body: Menopause before 45 is called early menopause, and before 40 premature menopause. Around one in ten women experience it. Causes include surgery to remove the ovaries, cancer treatment, some autoimmune or genetic conditions, and in about half of cases no cause is found. Symptoms can be more intense because the change is sudden. If your periods stop or change before 45, see your GP.

title: Premature ovarian insufficiency
body: Premature ovarian insufficiency, or POI, means the ovaries stop working normally before age 40. Periods may become irregular or stop, and pregnancy becomes much harder, though a small chance remains. POI is linked with some autoimmune conditions, like thyroid disease. Diagnosis involves blood tests. Hormone treatment is usually recommended until around 51 to protect bones and heart, and emotional support matters too.

title: Health risks of early menopause
body: Women with early or premature menopause have a higher risk of osteoporosis and heart disease, because they spend more years with low oestrogen. That's why hormone therapy, usually MHT or sometimes the contraceptive pill, is generally recommended until around age 51 unless there's a reason not to. Regular bone and heart checks are important even if you feel well. Your GP can plan a schedule of checks with you.

title: Emotional impact of early menopause
body: Early menopause can bring grief, shock, worries about fertility, body image and identity, and a sense of being out of step with friends. Higher rates of anxiety and low mood are reported. These feelings are understandable and valid. Talking with a psychologist, connecting with others who've been through it and involving your partner can help. Support organisations for POI and early menopause also exist.

title: Menopause after cancer treatment
body: Chemotherapy, radiotherapy to the pelvis and some hormone treatments for breast cancer can cause menopause, sometimes suddenly. Symptoms may be intense, and hormone therapy may not be suitable depending on the cancer. Non-hormonal medicines, vaginal moisturisers, CBT and hypnosis can help. Your cancer team, GP and organisations like the Cancer Council can guide you to the right support. You don't have to manage symptoms alone.

title: Fertility and early menopause
body: For women who hoped for children, early menopause or POI can be devastating. Natural pregnancy is unlikely but not impossible with POI. Options like IVF with donor eggs exist, and a fertility specialist can explain them. If you don't want to become pregnant, contraception is still advised with POI. Counselling can help you work through the emotions and decisions. Support groups can also help.

title: Medical menopause from medicines
body: Some medicines can temporarily or permanently stop the ovaries working, causing menopause-like symptoms. These include treatments for endometriosis, fibroids and some cancers. Symptoms may be sudden. Talk with your specialist about what to expect and how symptoms can be managed, which sometimes includes add-back hormone therapy. Keep a symptom record so your specialist can see how you're going. Ask what to expect when the treatment stops, as some effects may be temporary and others longer lasting.

title: When to see your GP about early changes
body: See your GP if your periods become irregular or stop before 45, if you're under 45 and haven't had a period for more than three months, or if you have menopausal symptoms at a younger age than expected. Early assessment means you can get the right tests and treatment, protecting your long-term health as well as easing symptoms. Bring your cycle record if you have one.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: The menopause health assessment
body: Since July 2025, Medicare has funded a dedicated menopause and perimenopause health assessment with your GP. It's a consultation of at least 20 minutes, available once every 12 months, for women in perimenopause, menopause or with early menopause or POI. It covers your symptoms, blood pressure and weight, screening and tests as needed, treatment options and a personalised plan. Ask for it by name when booking.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Preparing for your GP appointment
body: Before your appointment, jot down your main symptoms and how they affect your life, your period changes, your medicines and supplements, your family history and your questions. Bring a few months of tracking if you have it. Book a longer appointment if you can. Leading with what matters most helps your doctor focus on what you need. Pause and Play's GP summary can do much of this for you.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: What to say to your GP
body: It can help to start clearly: I think I might be in perimenopause, and it's affecting my sleep, mood and work. I'd like to talk about my options. Describe the impact on your life, not just the symptoms. If you feel brushed off, it's okay to ask for more time, a follow-up appointment or a second opinion. Bringing notes helps you stay on track.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: If you feel dismissed
body: Unfortunately some women feel their concerns aren't taken seriously. You deserve to be heard. Try bringing written notes, explaining how symptoms affect daily life, and asking directly about treatment options. If it still doesn't feel right, you can see another GP, ask for a referral, or look for a doctor with a special interest in menopause through the Australasian Menopause Society.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Your symptom diary
body: Health organisations recommend tracking symptoms and periods for at least three months before seeing your doctor. Note period dates and flow, hot flushes, sleep, mood and anything else that changes. Patterns over weeks tell a clearer story than memory alone. Pause and Play's Cycle Tracker and Mood Mapper can create a summary to bring along. Even brief daily notes are valuable.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Your pharmacist can help
body: Pharmacists are medicine experts and you don't need an appointment to talk with one. They can explain how to use patches, gels and pessaries, what to do if you miss a dose, possible side effects and interactions with other medicines and supplements. They can also advise on over-the-counter products like vaginal moisturisers. It's free and quick advice that many people underuse.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Healthdirect
body: Healthdirect is a free Australian government health advice line staffed by registered nurses, available 24 hours a day on 1800 022 222. Nurses can help you work out whether you need to see a GP, go to hospital or manage at home. The healthdirect website also has reliable information on menopause and its treatments. Their online symptom checker can also help you decide where to go. It's a useful first call if you're unsure whether something can wait.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Trusted information sources
body: For reliable Australian information, try the Australasian Menopause Society, Jean Hailes for Women's Health, healthdirect, and the Australian Government's perimenopause and menopause pages at health.gov.au. Be cautious with social media, where claims and product promotions can be misleading. If something sounds too good to be true, check with your GP or pharmacist. Pause and Play's Learn section draws on these organisations.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Menopause specialists
body: Most women are well cared for by their GP, but some benefit from a specialist, such as a gynaecologist or endocrinologist with menopause expertise, or a hospital menopause clinic. This can be helpful for complex health histories, early menopause, or when treatment isn't working. Your GP can refer you. The Australasian Menopause Society lists doctors with a special interest in menopause.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Allied health support
body: Other health professionals can help too. Psychologists support mood, anxiety, sleep and coping. Pelvic health physiotherapists help with bladder, pelvic floor and sexual pain. Accredited exercise physiologists design safe exercise programs. Accredited practising dietitians personalise eating plans. Your GP can tell you whether you're eligible for Medicare-subsidised sessions for some of these services. Ask your GP whether a chronic condition management plan applies to you, as this can make some of these services more affordable.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women
body: Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services offer culturally safe care, including women's health and menopause support, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Workers and Practitioners can be part of your care team. Health checks are available from earlier ages for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, including heart health checks from 30. Ask your health service what's available. 13YARN, 13 92 76, offers crisis support.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Getting support in your language
body: You can ask for a free interpreter when seeing a GP or other health professional; the Translating and Interpreting Service is available on 131 450. Jean Hailes and other health organisations provide menopause information in many languages. Bringing a trusted family member or friend can help too, but a professional interpreter is often best for private health conversations. Your GP's reception team can book one for you.

category: Seeing your GP and getting support
title: Online and community support
body: Connecting with others going through the same thing can be reassuring. Look for menopause support groups, workplace networks or community programs. Online communities can offer encouragement, but check information against trusted sources, as advice there isn't always accurate. The Pause and Play program offers a supportive group setting with qualified facilitators. Look for groups moderated by health professionals or reputable organisations. A good group leaves you feeling supported and better informed, not more anxious or pressured to buy products.

title: Menopause at work
body: Menopause affects many women at work. In one survey, most women in the transition said their work was affected, and many didn't feel comfortable telling their manager. Common challenges include hot flushes, poor sleep, brain fog and anxiety. You're not alone, and supportive workplaces are becoming more common. Practical adjustments and treatment can help you keep doing the work you value.

title: Talking to your manager
body: You don't have to share details, but if symptoms are affecting your work it can help to talk with your manager or HR. Focus on what would help: flexible start times, access to a fan or cooler workspace, breaks, working from home some days or written follow-ups after meetings. Preparing a few notes beforehand makes the conversation easier. You can share as much or as little as you like.

title: Workplace adjustments that help
body: Helpful adjustments can include temperature control or a desk fan, access to cold water and toilets, flexible hours on bad sleep days, the option to work from home, breathable uniforms, quiet spaces, and permission to step out during a hot flush. Many of these cost little and help everyone. Some Australian workplaces now have menopause policies; check whether yours does.

title: Thinking of leaving work?
body: Some women consider reducing hours, stepping back or leaving work because of menopausal symptoms. Before making a big decision, it may be worth exploring treatment and workplace adjustments, as symptoms often improve. If you do choose to make a change, let it be a decision you make freely, not one forced by symptoms that could be managed. A career counsellor or your union may also offer guidance.

title: Talking with your partner
body: Your partner can't support what they don't understand. Try explaining what you're experiencing and how it affects you, and what helps. Pause and Play's Learn section has information for partners. Let them know that irritability or low libido isn't about them, and invite them into the conversation as a teammate. Going to a GP appointment together can also help. Choose a calm time to talk, not mid-argument.

title: How partners can help
body: Partners can help by listening without trying to fix everything, learning about menopause, sharing more of the household and caring load, being patient about sex and intimacy, supporting healthy habits like less alcohol, coming to appointments if invited, and asking what would help today. Small, practical support often means more than grand gestures. Asking rather than assuming is one of the most helpful things a partner can do. Partners can find more ideas in the Learn section.

title: Relationships under strain
body: Sleep loss, irritability, low libido and feeling unlike yourself can put pressure on any relationship. It helps to name menopause as a shared challenge rather than a source of blame. Schedule time to connect that isn't about logistics. If tension keeps building, a relationship counsellor or psychologist can help you both communicate and reconnect. Seeking help early is a sign of commitment, not failure.

title: Parenting teenagers in perimenopause
body: Many women hit perimenopause just as their children hit puberty, which can make for a lot of hormones under one roof. Patience can run short on both sides. Being open with teenagers, in an age-appropriate way, that you're going through changes too can build understanding. Taking a pause before reacting, and repairing after a blow-up, models great skills for them.

title: Caring for ageing parents
body: Many women in midlife care for ageing parents as well as children, often while working. This sandwich role is exhausting and can intensify menopausal symptoms like poor sleep and overwhelm. Share the load where possible, accept help and look into carer supports such as Carer Gateway on 1800 422 737. Looking after yourself isn't selfish; it's what keeps you able to care for others.

title: Talking to friends
body: Many women don't talk about menopause, even with close friends, but opening up often reveals you're not alone. You might start with, has anyone else been waking at 3am? Sharing experiences and tips can bring relief and even laughter. If friends haven't reached this stage yet, your openness may help them feel more prepared. You might be the one who makes it easier for others to talk.

title: Telling family what you need
body: Families can be more supportive when they know what's going on and what helps. Be specific: I'm sleeping badly, so I need help with dinner on weeknights, or I need ten quiet minutes when I get home. Clear requests are easier to meet than hints. It's fine to ask for help repeatedly while you find your feet. Notice and thank people when they help.

title: Make a hot flush kit
body: Keep a small kit in your bag: a folding or handheld fan, a cooling face mist, a water bottle, a spare light top and some tissues or blotting papers. Having it with you can ease the worry about being caught out, and less worry can make flushes easier to manage. Add a hair tie if long hair makes you hotter, and keep a spare kit in the car or at your desk.

title: One home for important things
body: Choose one spot for the things you always lose, like keys, glasses, wallet and phone, and make it a habit to drop them there. A bowl by the door works for many people. When something's not there, check the Very Important Thing Department. Reducing the daily hunt saves time and frustration. Label it if that helps the whole household join in. It's a small habit that quietly saves minutes and frustration every single day.

title: The two-minute brain dump
body: When your head feels full, set a timer for two minutes and write down everything on your mind, without sorting it. Then circle just one thing to do next. Getting it out of your head reduces mental load, and choosing one action helps you move forward instead of spinning. Keep the list somewhere you'll see it, and transfer anything time-sensitive into Side Quest Saver or a reminder so it doesn't slip.

title: Protect your best hours
body: Notice when you feel sharpest, often in the morning, and protect that time for tasks that need focus. Save easier tasks, like email or admin, for times you feel foggier. Working with your energy rather than against it can make a big difference on days when sleep has been poor. Block that time in your calendar if you can, and let colleagues know when you're doing focused work.

title: Say it, then write it
body: When someone tells you something important, repeat it back aloud, then write it down or tell Sprout straight away. Saying it helps encode the memory, and writing it means you don't have to rely on remembering. This simple habit is especially useful for appointments, names and instructions. A quick voice note to Sprout takes seconds. It's especially handy when your hands are full, like in the car park or at the pharmacy counter.

title: Layers, layers, layers
body: Dressing in layers is one of the simplest ways to manage temperature swings. Choose a breathable base layer of cotton, linen or bamboo, with an easy-to-remove top layer. Avoid tight necklines and synthetic fabrics that trap heat. Keep a light cardigan for air-conditioned rooms and peel off when a flush hits. Natural fibres breathe better and help sweat evaporate, so you cool down faster.

title: Make bedtime boring
body: A predictable, slightly boring bedtime routine tells your brain it's time to wind down. Same time, same steps: dim the lights, put the phone away, a warm shower, a few pages of a gentle book, then lights out. Keep the bedroom for sleep and intimacy, not work or scrolling. Consistency matters more than any single step, so choose things you can realistically keep doing most nights.

title: Try one alcohol-free week
body: Alcohol can worsen hot flushes, sleep and mood. Try a week without it and notice how you sleep and feel, using Mood Mapper to keep track. Many women are surprised by the difference. If you enjoy a drink, alcohol-free alternatives and setting a few alcohol-free days each week are easy places to start. Notice any change in hot flushes as well as sleep.

title: Move a little, often
body: You don't need long workouts to feel the benefits of movement. A ten-minute walk after meals, stretching while the kettle boils, or taking the stairs all add up. Movement can lift mood, help sleep, ease joint stiffness and clear a foggy head. Two short bursts of strength work each week help muscles and bones too. Find movement you enjoy and it stops feeling like a chore.

title: Prepare for tricky days
body: If your mood or symptoms follow a pattern, use it. On days you expect to be harder, lighten your schedule, prepare easy meals ahead, ask for help early and plan something soothing. Planning for tricky days isn't giving in; it's working smarter with what your body is doing. Cycle Tracker and Mood Mapper can help you spot when those days tend to come. Letting the people around you know in advance can make a real difference too.

title: Keep a cool drink handy
body: A cold drink can help you ride out a hot flush and keep you hydrated. Keep a water bottle at your desk, in the car and by the bed. Some women find avoiding hot drinks during flush-prone times helps too. Staying hydrated also supports energy, concentration and joint comfort. Add ice, cucumber or mint to make water more appealing, and set a gentle reminder if you often forget to drink.

title: Use reminders without shame
body: Phone reminders, sticky notes, alarms and lists aren't signs of failing; they're smart tools that free up mental space. Many people with busy lives use them constantly. Set reminders for medicines, appointments and tasks, and let Pause and Play's Today list carry some of the load. The goal is less to remember, not more willpower. Choose a few reminders that genuinely help, and switch off any that just add noise.

title: The pause before reacting
body: When you feel a surge of irritation, try a three-second pause: one long breath out before you speak. It creates just enough space to choose your response. If you do snap, it's okay; a quick repair like, sorry, I'm running on empty today, goes a long way in keeping relationships strong. Practising this when you're calm makes it easier to use when you're not.

title: Batch the small stuff
body: Lots of little tasks can drain a foggy brain. Try batching them: one time each day for emails, one for bills, one for messages. This reduces the mental cost of switching between tasks. Park anything that pops up in between with Side Quest Saver, so it's not lost. Choose a time when your energy is moderate, not your best hours, and keep the batch short so it doesn't become another chore.

title: Cool your pulse points
body: When a hot flush starts, cooling your wrists, the back of your neck or your temples with cold water or a cool pack can feel especially relieving. Some women keep a damp cloth in a sealed bag in the fridge. It won't stop the flush, but it can make it more comfortable. Cooling towels designed for sport work well too.

title: Laugh about it, together
body: Sharing the funny side with friends who get it, like the glasses on your head or the fridge-dwelling keys, can turn frustration into connection. Humour doesn't make symptoms disappear, but it can make them lighter to carry. The I need a laugh section is there for exactly those moments. Sharing stories also reminds you that you're far from alone in this.

title: You're not alone
body: Millions of women are going through perimenopause and menopause right now. In Australia, it's a natural stage that every woman who reaches midlife will move through. Whatever you're feeling, others have felt it too. Reaching for information and support, as you're doing now, is a sign of care for yourself. Women all over Australia are asking the same questions, and talking about it more openly than ever before.

title: This stage won't last forever
body: Perimenopause is a transition, and transitions end. For many women, symptoms ease after menopause, and many describe feeling more confident, settled and free in the years that follow. While you're in the thick of it, support and treatment can make the journey much easier. Keep a note of what helps, so you can lean on it on harder days. Each small step you take now makes the road ahead a little easier.

title: You're doing better than you think
body: If you're juggling symptoms, work, family and everything else, and still showing up, that's worth acknowledging. Perimenopause can make you feel less capable than you are. Try listing three things you managed today, however small. They count. Write them down or say them out loud. On hard days it's easy to only notice what went wrong, so practising noticing what went right helps balance the picture. You are coping with more than most people can see.

title: Progress, not perfection
body: Looking after yourself doesn't have to be all or nothing. A short walk counts. One alcohol-free night counts. Parking one task instead of losing it counts. Small steps, repeated, make real change. Your garden in Pause and Play grows the same way: one petal at a time. If you miss a day, simply start again; nothing is lost, and every fresh start counts.

title: It's okay to rest
body: Rest isn't laziness; it's part of looking after your health. When sleep has been broken or your energy is low, giving yourself permission to slow down helps your body and mind recover. Lower the bar for a day, say no to something, and let that be enough. Rest is productive when it helps you keep going. A short pause now can save you from running on empty later.

title: Your feelings make sense
body: Feeling frustrated, sad, angry or unsettled during perimenopause makes sense. Your body is changing, sleep may be disrupted and life is often busy. Feelings aren't problems to fix straight away; they're information. Naming how you feel, even in Mood Mapper, is a good first step toward working out what you need. You don't need to justify how you feel to anyone.

title: Asking for help is strong
body: Asking for help is a skill and a strength, not a weakness. Whether it's booking a GP appointment, telling your partner what you need or asking a colleague to take something on, reaching out makes the load lighter. The people who care about you usually want to help; they just need to know how. Try one specific, small request today.

title: Celebrate small wins
body: Did you remember your medicine? Find your keys on the first try? Get through a meeting despite a hot flush? Celebrate it. Noticing small wins builds confidence and motivation, especially on days when everything feels hard. Your badges and garden are little reminders of the effort you're putting in. Tell someone about one of them today, or simply pause and notice it yourself.

title: Be gentle with yourself today
body: If today feels heavy, be gentle with yourself. Do the essentials, let the rest wait, and do one thing that brings a little comfort: a cup of tea in the sun, a call to a friend, a few slow breaths. Tomorrow is a new start. Hard days pass. Notice the small comforts available to you, and remember that you've made it through every hard day so far.

title: There is help that works
body: You don't have to just put up with symptoms. Hormone therapy, non-hormonal medicines, CBT, hypnosis, practical strategies and lifestyle changes all have evidence behind them, and most women can find something that helps. If the first thing you try doesn't suit, there are other options to explore with your doctor. Finding the right fit can take time, so keep going.

title: A new chapter
body: Many women find that menopause, once the hardest parts settle, opens a new chapter. Without periods, contraception worries or monthly hormone swings, some feel freer and more confident. It can be a time to reconnect with what matters, try new things and prioritise yourself. The transition is real, and so is the possibility on the other side. Many women look back on this time as the start of something good.

title: Your body is doing something remarkable
body: Your body has carried you through decades of change, and menopause is another big shift it's navigating. Instead of seeing it as breaking down, try seeing it as adapting. Treat it with the care you'd give someone you love: good food, movement, rest, and support when it needs it. Notice one thing your body did for you today, whether that's carrying you through a busy day, healing a scrape or simply letting you breathe out slowly.

title: One thing at a time
body: When everything feels urgent, remember you can only do one thing at a time anyway. Choose the next small step, do it, then choose the next. That's how big things get done, and it's a lot kinder on a busy brain than trying to hold everything at once. The 37 tabs tool is a playful way to practise this. Close what can wait, keep what matters, and let the rest come later.

title: You're allowed to say no
body: Midlife often comes with more demands than ever. Saying no to some requests means saying yes to your health, sleep and sanity. A simple, I can't take that on right now, is enough. Protecting your energy during a demanding transition is wise, not selfish. You can always say yes later if things change. Practise a few phrases in advance so a kind, clear no comes more easily when you need it.

title: Morning motivation
body: Good morning. Whatever last night was like, today is a fresh start. Pick one thing that would make today a little easier, and one small thing just for you. You don't have to do it all; you just have to do the next thing. A glass of water, a little daylight and a few slow breaths are a lovely way to begin. Check Today for what's due, and let the rest of the day unfold one step at a time.

title: Evening reflection
body: Before bed, try noticing three things: one thing that went okay today, one thing you're grateful for, and one thing you can let go of until tomorrow. This simple reflection can help your mind settle and shift attention from what went wrong to what went right. Over time, this practice can gently shift how you see your days. You might like to pair it with a wind-down session to help your body settle too.

title: Your experience matters
body: Women's experiences of menopause were overlooked for a long time. That's changing in Australia, with new Medicare-funded assessments, more affordable treatments and growing awareness. Your experience matters, and you deserve care that takes it seriously. Speaking up, for yourself and others, is part of that change. Sharing your story, even with one friend, helps break the silence. When more women talk openly, it becomes easier for everyone to ask for the care they deserve.

title: Laughter is allowed
body: Perimenopause can be hard, and it can also be absurd. Keys in the fridge, coffee reheated three times, glasses on your head. Finding the funny side doesn't mean you're not taking it seriously; it means you're coping. Share a laugh with someone who gets it today. The I need a laugh section is there whenever you need it. Laughing at the situation, never at yourself, can take the sting out of a frustrating day.

title: Taking care of you
body: You probably spend a lot of time looking after others. This is a reminder that you deserve the same care. Book that appointment, take that walk, eat that proper lunch, go to bed a little earlier. Looking after yourself is how you keep going for everyone else, and for you. Choose one small act of care for yourself today, and enjoy it.

title: Myth: you just have to put up with it
body: Fact: there are many evidence-based treatments and supports for perimenopause and menopause, from hormone therapy and non-hormonal medicines to CBT, hypnosis and practical strategies. You don't have to endure symptoms that affect your life. Talking with your GP is a good first step. Treatment options have expanded in recent years, including new non-hormonal medicines and more affordable hormone therapy on the PBS. Support is also available from psychologists, pharmacists and specialist clinics.

title: Myth: everyone has a terrible time
body: Fact: experiences vary widely. About one in four women have few or no symptoms, about half have mild to moderate symptoms, and about one in four have severe symptoms. Your experience is your own, and it's not a reflection of how well you're coping. If you are struggling, support and treatment can help, and if you are sailing through, that's normal too. Neither experience means you're doing it right or wrong.

title: Myth: menopause only matters in your 60s
body: Fact: the average age of menopause in Australia is 51, and perimenopause often begins in your 40s. Some women experience early menopause or POI even younger. Learning about these changes earlier helps you recognise them and look after your health sooner. If your periods change or stop before 45, see your GP, as earlier assessment protects your long-term health. Midlife is also a great time for a full health check.

title: Myth: hot flushes are the only symptom
body: Fact: hot flushes are common, but menopause can also bring sleep problems, mood changes, anxiety, brain fog, joint aches, lower libido, vaginal dryness and bladder changes. Recognising the wider range of symptoms helps you get the right support. Because symptoms are so varied, many women don't connect them to perimenopause at first. Tracking them over a few months can help you and your GP see the bigger picture.

title: Myth: you can't get pregnant in perimenopause
body: Fact: pregnancy is still possible while you're having periods, even irregular ones. Contraception is generally recommended until two years after your last period if you're under 50, or one year if you're over 50. Hormone therapy isn't a contraceptive. Your GP can help you choose contraception that suits your stage of life, and some options, like the hormonal IUD, can also help with heavy periods or form part of hormone therapy.

title: Myth: a blood test can tell if you're in menopause
body: Fact: for women over 45, doctors usually diagnose perimenopause and menopause based on age, symptoms and period changes. Hormone levels fluctuate so much that a single test can be misleading. Blood tests are useful for younger women or to rule out other causes. Home hormone and saliva tests aren't recommended either. Tracking your periods and symptoms, and talking them through with your GP, gives a clearer picture than a single test.

title: Myth: natural remedies are always safer
body: Fact: natural doesn't guarantee safe or effective. Some herbal products can interact with medicines or be unsuitable with certain conditions, and quality varies. Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for hot flushes. Check any natural product with your GP or pharmacist. In Australia, look for an AUST L or AUST R number on supplement labels, and be cautious with products bought online from overseas.

title: Myth: life goes downhill after menopause
body: Fact: while symptoms can be challenging, many women report greater confidence, freedom and focus after menopause. With support, lifestyle strategies and treatment, quality of life can be good, and for many it improves. Many women find this stage brings a new sense of freedom, without monthly cycles or contraception worries. Looking after your health now helps you make the most of the decades ahead.

title: Myth: every woman becomes moody
body: Fact: mood changes are common but not universal. When they happen, hormonal changes play a part, along with sleep, stress, caring responsibilities and work. Mood changes are understandable, not a character flaw, and support is available. If mood changes are affecting your life, talking with your GP or a psychologist can help. Tracking your moods in Mood Mapper can also show whether they follow a pattern.

title: Myth: breast cancer is the biggest health risk after menopause
body: Fact: many women fear breast cancer most, but heart disease and stroke cause more deaths in postmenopausal women. Breast cancer is important, and screening matters, but looking after your heart through activity, healthy eating, not smoking and managing blood pressure and cholesterol is just as vital. A Heart Health Check with your GP is recommended from age 45, or from 30 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: In a crisis
body: If you're in immediate danger or need urgent medical help, call 000. If you're having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, text 0477 13 11 14 or chat online at lifeline.org.au, any time of day or night. Pause and Play, including Sprout, can't respond to emergencies. Please reach out to real people now. If you can, also let someone near you know.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: Bleeding that needs checking
body: See your GP about very heavy periods, bleeding between periods, bleeding after sex, or any vaginal bleeding after your periods have stopped for 12 months. On MHT, persistent or unexpected bleeding after the first six months should also be checked. Most causes aren't serious, but these signs always need assessment. Cycle Tracker can help you record exactly what's happening, which makes it easier to describe to your doctor.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: Symptoms that need urgent care
body: Call 000 for chest pain, sudden breathlessness, signs of stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech, or severe sudden headache. See a doctor urgently for leg pain and swelling, especially in one calf, which can be a sign of a blood clot. Don't wait or put these down to menopause. Trust your instincts and seek help quickly; it's always better to be checked.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: Mental health support lines
body: You don't need to be in crisis to reach out. Lifeline, 13 11 14, is available 24/7. Beyond Blue, 1300 22 4636, offers support for anxiety and depression. The Suicide Call Back Service is on 1300 659 467. 13YARN, 13 92 76, supports Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Your GP can also help you access ongoing support. Calls are confidential.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: Family and domestic violence support
body: If you're experiencing violence or feel unsafe at home, help is available. Call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732, any time, for confidential support. In an emergency, call 000. Stress and relationship changes in midlife can sometimes coincide with abuse; you deserve to be safe. You can also talk with your GP, who can help you plan for your safety. Services can be accessed confidentially, and support is available in many languages.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: Breast changes to check
body: See your GP promptly about any new breast lump or thickening, changes in breast size or shape, nipple changes or discharge, skin dimpling or redness, or ongoing pain in one spot. Most changes aren't cancer, but they always need checking. Keep up with free BreastScreen mammograms from age 50. Know what's normal for you by noticing how your breasts usually look and feel, so changes are easier to spot early.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: Medicine safety
body: Keep a current list of all your medicines and supplements, including doses, and share it with every doctor and pharmacist you see. Read the consumer medicine information leaflet for each one. Don't start, stop or change prescription medicines without advice. Medicine Cabinet can help you keep your list up to date. Update it whenever something changes, and keep a copy on your phone so it's with you at every appointment, including emergencies.

category: Safety and when to get help
title: When Sprout can't help
body: Sprout can share general information from the Pause and Play library, but it can't assess your situation. For anything personal about symptoms, medicines, tests or treatment decisions, please see your GP, pharmacist or specialist. If you're unsure whether something is urgent, healthdirect's nurses are available 24/7 on 1800 022 222. Sprout will always be honest when something is outside what it can help with. Your health professionals know your history and can give advice that's right for you.
